q: Which of the following best states what the passage mainly explains?
o: How drivers can avoid damaging their tyres on long bridges
Why steel is preferred to concrete for long bridge decks
How careless road-laying causes bumps on long bridges
Why long bridges are built with gaps that let their sections move
x: The passage explains that decks grow and shrink with temperature and that expansion joints leave "a deliberate gap that can open and close". The bumps are not caused by bad road-laying; the first paragraph says the strips are "placed there on purpose".

q: According to the passage, what would happen to a long deck fixed rigidly at both ends?
o: It would sag in the middle under the weight of heavy traffic
It would stay the same length in summer and in winter
It would strain its supports as it heated and cooled, and crack over time
It would bend sideways whenever a strong wind blew
x: The second paragraph says such a deck would push on its supports in the heat and pull on them in the cold, and "this repeated strain would crack the concrete". It would not stay the same length: the deck "can lengthen by many centimetres".

q: The passage suggests that a bridge in a place with very hot summers and very cold winters would need:
o: narrower expansion joints, so that the road stays smooth
wider expansion joints than a similar bridge in a mild climate
fewer expansion joints, because the changes cancel each other out
a deck fixed more firmly to the banks at both ends
x: Engineers "calculate the widest gap the local climate could demand", so bigger temperature swings mean a wider gap. Narrower joints are wrong: "a joint that is too narrow is almost worse than none at all".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "rigidly" most nearly means:
o: strictly, without bending any rules
loosely, with room to slide
firmly, so that no movement is possible
quickly, before the material warms
x: A deck fixed "rigidly" leaves the material with "nowhere to go", so the word means firmly, with no movement. "Strictly" is the word's meaning for rules and behaviour, not for how a deck is attached.

q: What does the second paragraph do in the passage?
o: It describes the shape of the teeth on an expansion joint
It argues that concrete bridges are no longer safe to use
It corrects the drivers' belief that the road was badly laid
It explains the cause of the problem that the joint, described next, solves
x: The second paragraph explains how heat and cold make a deck grow and shrink, and the third begins "The joint solves the problem". Correcting the drivers' belief is done in the first paragraph ("placed there on purpose").

q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: How Mud and Paint Dry in the Sun
The Dangers of Building Roofs in Summer
Why Concrete Must Be Kept Wet to Gain Strength
Why Labourers Work Slowly on Building Sites
x: The whole passage explains that concrete hardens by hydration and that curing "allows it to reach the strength it was designed for". Mud and paint are mentioned only once, as a contrast.

q: According to the passage, concrete becomes hard because:
o: the water in the mix slowly evaporates in the sun
the sand and stones are pressed together as it dries
a coating is sprayed over its surface by labourers
cement reacts chemically with water and forms crystals
x: The second paragraph says concrete "hardens through a chemical reaction between cement and water, called hydration, in which tiny crystals grow". Evaporation is the passer-by's mistaken idea: concrete "does not harden by drying".

q: What is most likely true of a slab left uncovered in hot sun just after it is poured?
o: It will reach its full strength sooner than a slab kept damp
The heat will soften it so that it must be poured again at once
Its whole depth will crumble to dust within a few days
Its surface may end up weaker than the concrete beneath it
x: If the surface dries early, "hydration near the top stops", leaving "a weak, dusty skin", so the top is weaker than the rest. Crumbling through its whole depth in days goes too far: the passage speaks of the top and of cracks "within months".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "knit" most nearly means:
o: join firmly together
make clothes from wool
pull slowly apart
cover with a thin layer
x: The crystals "knit the sand and stones together", that is, they bind them into one solid. Making clothes from wool is the word's everyday meaning, not the one used here.

q: In the third paragraph, the word "therefore" shows that the sentence it begins:
o: contrasts curing with the way that mud and paint dry
introduces an example of a mistake made on a busy site
draws a conclusion from the account of hydration just given
repeats the passer-by's view that watering is pointless
x: "Therefore" signals a result: because hydration needs water, keeping concrete damp lets it reach its strength. It does not repeat the passer-by's view; it overturns it by saying curing "does not soften it".

q: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
o: To prove that wind turbines are better than solar panels
To explain in detail how batteries store electricity
To show how weighing two energy sources led to choosing a mix of both
To criticise the council for wasting time in debate
x: The passage compares panels and turbines and ends with Farah's "modest mix of the two". It does not prove turbines better; Farah "refused to declare a winner".

q: According to the passage, one advantage of solar panels is that they:
o: go on producing power after dark
need very little care to keep working
work best on long winter nights
cost less to build than turbines
x: The second paragraph says panels "have no moving parts" and "need little more than an occasional wash". Power after dark is wrong: they produce "nothing at all after dark", and cost is never compared.

q: Farah's point about the ridge and the cloudy months suggests that combining panels and turbines would:
o: remove any need for batteries in the village
cost less than building solar panels alone
produce the most power at noon in winter
give a steadier supply through the year than either source alone
x: The ridge is windiest when the valley is cloudiest, so the two sources "tended to fall short at different times" and together fill each other's gaps. Batteries are still needed: her plan includes "a bank of batteries to cover the quiet hours".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "temperamental" most nearly means:
o: quick to lose one's temper
dependent on the air temperature
unpredictable and harder to manage
made of fragile materials
x: Turbines are called "temperamental" because "the wind rises and falls without warning" and they "need skilled care". Losing one's temper is the meaning for people, and the passage never links turbines to temperature.

q: The writer's attitude towards Farah's recommendation is best described as:
o: disappointed, because it did not name a clear winner
approving, because it was practical even if not exciting
mocking, because it was far too cautious
doubtful, because batteries are often unreliable
x: The writer calls Farah "patient" and ends by saying her answer "was the one that kept the lights on", which is praise. The disappointment belongs to "some councillors", not to the writer.

q: The passage mainly explains:
o: why the delay between seeing and hearing something shows how far away it is
how a flash of lightning produces the sound of thunder
why children are frightened of storms during the monsoon
how warm air makes sound travel much faster
x: Light arrives "almost instantly" while sound takes about three seconds per kilometre, so the gap measures distance, for storms and at cricket grounds. How lightning makes thunder is never explained.

q: According to the passage, how does sound travel?
o: Almost instantly, at the same speed as light
As a narrow beam that only wind can bend
At about three kilometres every second
As a wave passed from one layer of air molecules to the next
x: The second paragraph says sound "moves as a wave of squeezed and stretched air, passed from one layer of molecules to the next". It covers "roughly one kilometre in three seconds", not three kilometres a second.

q: A spectator sitting very close to the pitch would most likely:
o: notice a much shorter delay, or none, between seeing and hearing the shot
hear the crack of the bat before seeing the ball being hit
notice a longer delay than a spectator far from the pitch
be unable to hear the crack of the bat at all
x: The delay grows with distance because "the sound is simply still on its way", so a nearby spectator would notice little or no gap. Hearing first is impossible by the passage, since light arrives "almost instantly".

q: As used in the fourth paragraph, the word "nudge" most nearly means:
o: push with the elbow
reverse completely
change slightly
measure exactly
x: Wind and temperature "nudge the speed of sound up or down a little", so the word means change it slightly. Pushing with the elbow is its everyday physical meaning.

q: In the last paragraph, the writer's attitude towards the counting rule is best described as:
o: appreciative, valuing it in spite of its limits
dismissive, because it gives only a rough answer
anxious, because storms are frightening
uncritical, treating it as perfectly exact
x: The writer admits "The rule has its limits" but calls it "remarkably reliable" with "the rare virtue" of calming fear. It is not treated as exact, since wind and temperature change the speed of sound.

q: Which title best sums up the passage?
o: How Memory Chips Are Made in Factories
The History of Counting with Ten Digits
How a Phone Stores a Photograph
Why Computers Store Everything in Twos
x: The passage explains that computers use only two states, why this is reliable, and how many bits make up for it. Photographs are named only as one example of what is stored.

q: According to the passage, engineers prefer switches with only two states because:
o: two-state switches are cheaper to manufacture
the two states can still be told apart when the voltage wobbles
people find binary numbers easier to read than ordinary ones
two-state switches use less electricity than others
x: The second paragraph says a two-state switch "can tolerate a good deal of electrical noise; a small wobble in voltage will not change a 1 into a 0". Cost and electricity use are never mentioned.

q: The passage suggests that a switch built to hold ten different levels would:
o: be more likely to store a wrong value when disturbed
be able to store songs but not photographs
be unable to hold the digits 7 and 8 at all
be less affected by electrical noise than a two-state switch
x: Such a switch would have to tell levels apart "precisely", and "the slightest disturbance could turn a 7 into an 8", so errors are more likely. Being less affected by noise is the opposite: it is the two-state switch that "can tolerate a good deal of electrical noise".

q: As used in the last sentence, the word "humble" most nearly means:
o: simple and basic
not proud of one's own success
poor and unhappy
hidden and secret
x: The "humble foundation" is explained as "very simple choices", so the word means simple and basic. Not being proud of one's success is the meaning of the word for people.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: The third gives an example that contradicts the claim made in the second
The third repeats the point of the second in simpler words
The second describes a problem that the third says has not yet been solved
The second gives the advantage of using two states; the third shows how the system makes up for their limits
x: The second paragraph explains why two states are reliable; the third opens "What each switch lacks in range, the system makes up in sheer quantity". It does not contradict the second; it builds on it.

q: What is the writer mainly trying to do in the passage?
o: To argue that air conditioners should no longer be sold
To describe the history of house-building in Multan
To suggest low-cost ways of keeping homes in hot cities cooler
To show that concrete is the best material for hot cities
x: After describing the problem, the passage offers "remedies" that are "surprisingly cheap": white roofs, shade and old design ideas. It criticises air conditioners but never says they should be banned; it hopes they will "work less hard".

q: According to the passage, a white roof stays cooler because it:
o: lets heat escape more quickly at night
reflects much of the sunlight instead of soaking it up
is built thicker than a dark roof
is shaded by creepers and trees
x: The second paragraph says dark surfaces "soak up most of the sunlight" while white ones "reflect much of it back into the sky". Creepers and trees are a separate remedy, not the reason a white roof is cool.

q: What does the passage suggest about why many traditional cooling features disappeared?
o: They were found to make houses hotter at night
They cost more to build than air conditioners
They were dropped for reasons of space and fashion, not because they failed
They were forbidden by the rules of the cities
x: Builders abandoned them "partly because they took up space and partly because they looked old-fashioned", and the passage presents them as useful "lessons". Nothing says they made houses hotter.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "strain" most nearly means:
o: pass a liquid through a filter
put heavy pressure on
cut off completely
share out fairly
x: Air conditioners "strain the electricity supply during the hottest hours", that is, they load it heavily. Passing a liquid through a filter is the kitchen meaning of the word.

q: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as:
o: enthusiastic, promising that summers will become pleasant
hopeless, doubting that the measures will help at all
realistic, promising modest but useful benefits
angry with the builders who gave up old designs
x: The writer admits "None of these measures will make a June afternoon pleasant" but says they can lower temperatures "enough to let people sleep". That limit rules out the enthusiastic reading, and the claimed benefit rules out the hopeless one.

q: What is the main argument of the passage?
o: Old machines were always better made than modern ones
Glued cases are necessary to keep dust out of machines
Electronic waste should be sent abroad to be handled
Machines should be designed so that they can be repaired easily
x: The writer says "Engineers should treat repairability as a basic requirement" and explains how. The passage does not claim old machines were always better; the grandfather's fan is one example.

q: What reason do manufacturers give for sealed designs?
o: They make repairs quicker for mechanics
They let customers buy parts in the bazaar
They reduce the amount of electronic waste
They protect the device from dust and water
x: The second paragraph says: "Glued cases, they say, keep out dust and water". Sealed designs make repairs harder, not quicker, and the writer links them to more waste, not less.

q: The writer suggests that one reason manufacturers make devices hard to open is that:
o: glued cases are cheaper for them than screws
they earn more when customers buy new devices than when they repair old ones
customers have asked for devices that cannot be opened
laws in many places forbid them to sell spare parts
x: Right after the manufacturers' defence, the writer adds that "replacement is far more profitable than repair" and "Customers pay twice", hinting at a motive they do not state. Cost of glue, customer demand and laws are never mentioned.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "faltered" most nearly means:
o: spoke in a hesitant voice
was sold to a new owner
began to work unsteadily
grew noticeably louder
x: When the fan "faltered", a mechanic replaced "a worn bearing", so it had begun to fail. Speaking hesitantly is the word's meaning for a person's voice, which cannot apply to a fan.

q: The writer's attitude towards the manufacturers' defence of sealed designs is best described as:
o: fully convinced and supportive
completely dismissive, calling it untrue
uninterested and without any opinion
partly accepting but mainly unconvinced
x: The writer grants "Some of this is true" and then answers with "But", arguing that sealed products must be replaced. Calling the defence wholly untrue is wrong because of that admission.

q: What is the passage chiefly about?
o: why bus engines are louder than most other machines
how headphones can reduce noise by producing an opposite sound wave
why playing loud music harms a listener's hearing
how microphones are used to record music
x: The passage describes how the headphones copy the noise, turn the wave "upside down" and play it so the two cancel. Loud music is mentioned only as what ordinary earphones do.

q: According to the passage, what does the microphone on each ear cup do?
o: It records the listener's own voice
It plays the music into the ear
It blocks sudden and high-pitched sounds
It picks up the noise around the listener
x: The third paragraph says the microphone "listens to the surrounding noise". Blocking sudden sounds is done by "the padding of the ear cups", not the microphone.

q: Which of these sounds would the headphones most likely reduce best?
o: a dog barking suddenly nearby
a sharp whistle blown on a platform
the steady hum of a large ceiling fan
a plate crashing to the floor
x: The trick "works best on steady, low sounds" that change slowly. A sudden bark, a high whistle and a crash are the kinds of sound that "slip through".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "exploit" most nearly means:
o: make use of
treat unfairly for profit
explain clearly
try to avoid
x: The headphones "exploit this second case", that is, they put the cancelling of waves to work. Treating someone unfairly for profit is a common meaning of the word, but nobody is being wronged here.

q: In the third paragraph, the phrase "this second case" refers to:
o: the peaks of one wave meeting the troughs of another so that they cancel
the peaks of two waves lining up so that the sound grows louder
the second microphone, on the other ear cup
ordinary earphones playing music louder to cover noise
x: The second paragraph gives two cases; the second, introduced by "If, instead", is when peaks meet troughs and "they cancel out". Peaks lining up is the first case, which makes sound louder.

q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Copper should replace aluminium in all overhead power lines
Aluminium carries electricity better than any other metal
Copper and aluminium each suit a different use because of their properties
Wiring inside houses is more dangerous than overhead lines
x: The passage weighs each metal's strengths and ends: "Each is the right answer to a different question." It says copper is "the better conductor", so aluminium is not the best.

q: According to the passage, copper is preferred inside houses because it:
o: conducts well and can be bent many times without cracking
is lighter and cheaper than aluminium
never warms up when a current flows through it
has to be made thicker than aluminium to carry a current
x: Copper "wastes less energy as heat" and "can be bent many times without cracking, which matters in a house". It is heavier and dearer, not lighter and cheaper; it is aluminium that must be made thicker.

q: It can be inferred that if copper cables were used for long overhead lines:
o: the cables would need to be thicker than aluminium ones
the lines would waste more energy as heat
the towers would probably need to be stronger or more numerous
the joints would loosen and start fires
x: Copper is heavier, and "lighter cables need fewer and less massive towers", so heavier cables would need more or stronger towers. Copper wastes less heat, not more, and needs less thickness than aluminium.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "decisive" most nearly means:
o: settling the choice
quick to make up one's mind
dangerous
of little importance
x: Over long distances "this lightness is decisive", meaning it settles the choice in favour of aluminium. Quick to make up one's mind describes a person, not a property of a metal.

q: In the last paragraph, the writer's point of view is best described as:
o: biased in favour of copper
critical of engineers for using aluminium
unsure which metal conducts electricity better
balanced, seeing each metal as right for its own task
x: The writer says "Neither metal, then, is simply better than the other". The writer is not unsure about conduction: the second paragraph states "Copper is the better conductor".

q: Which of these would make the best title for the passage?
o: Why Food Spoils Quickly in Hot Weather
How Sweat Cools the Human Body
Moving Heat: How a Refrigerator Works
The Dangers of a Noisy Compressor
x: The passage says a fridge does not make cold but moves heat, then follows the refrigerant through the cabinet, compressor and outside pipes. Sweat is used only as a comparison.

q: According to the passage, where does the refrigerant give up its heat?
o: Inside the cabinet, into the air and food
In thin pipes on the outside of the fridge, into the room
Inside the compressor, into its motor
In a separate tank under the cabinet
x: The third paragraph says the refrigerant "flows through a grid of thin pipes on the outside of the fridge, gives up its heat to the room". Inside the cabinet it takes heat in, not out.

q: The passage suggests that a fridge pushed so tightly against a wall that air cannot reach its outside pipes would:
o: cool the food inside faster than usual
stop the refrigerant evaporating inside the cabinet
have more difficulty getting rid of the heat it collects
help to keep the kitchen cooler
x: Heat leaves the fridge through the pipes on the outside, which give "up its heat to the room"; with no air around them, that step becomes harder. Nothing in the passage suggests faster cooling or a cooler kitchen.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "circulates" most nearly means:
o: flows round and round
spreads among people
slowly cools down
stays in one place
x: The refrigerant "circulates endlessly through a loop of pipes", so it flows round and round. Spreading among people is the meaning used for news or rumours.

q: What does the last paragraph do in the passage?
o: It uses the explanation to correct a common mistaken belief
It introduces a part of the fridge not mentioned before
It argues that fridges waste too much electricity
It explains how to repair a fridge door that will not close
x: It opens "This explains a common mistake" and shows why an open fridge cannot cool a kitchen. No new part is introduced; the motor was already described in the third paragraph.

q: Which best states the writer's main purpose?
o: To argue that tube wells should be banned across Balochistan
To explain how a karez works and why it is now under threat
To describe how the shafts of a karez were dug by hand
To compare the cost of a karez with that of an open canal
x: The passage explains the design ("cleverer than it looks") and then its weakness, falling water tables caused by tube wells. It never calls for a ban across the province; it only says some communities limit new wells near their karez.

q: According to the first paragraph, what were the vertical shafts used for?
o: Letting sunlight and air dry out the tunnel
Letting farmers lift water straight up to their fields
Marking the borders between different families' land
Letting workers get into the tunnel and remove soil
x: Workers used the shafts "to lower themselves into the tunnel and to haul out the earth they removed". The shafts mark the route of the tunnel, not the borders of anyone's land.

q: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
o: A few dry winters in the hills could reduce a karez's flow
Tube wells cost less to run than a karez does
Open canals were never used in Balochistan
The rota of hours was agreed only after tube wells arrived
x: A karez delivers water only "as long as the aquifer that feeds it is replenished by rain and snow in the hills", so less rain and snow would mean less water. The rota is something families "once shared", so it came before the tube wells, not after them.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "replenished" most nearly means:
o: polluted
refilled
emptied
measured
x: The aquifer is fed by "rain and snow", and the third paragraph says tube wells take water out faster than it "can recover", so replenished means filled up again. "Emptied" is the opposite: that is what the tube wells do.

q: In the third paragraph, the phrase "That same dependence" refers to the karez's
o: reliance on an aquifer that must be refilled by rain and snow
reliance on electric pumps to lift water to the fields
dependence on the summer sun to warm its water
dependence on workers climbing down its shafts
x: The sentence before it says a karez works "as long as the aquifer that feeds it is replenished"; the third paragraph then shows the danger of that reliance when the water table falls. A karez was built "long before electric pumps" and needs no fuel.

q: Which is the best title for the passage?
o: Why Glaciers Are Growing in the North
Preparing for Floods from Glacial Lakes
How Mobile Networks Save Mountain Villages
The Beauty of High Mountain Lakes
x: The passage describes how glacial lakes burst and then the warnings, drills and controlled drainage that reduce the damage. Glaciers are melting, not growing, and the mobile network is mentioned only as something that may fail.

q: According to the first paragraph, the lakes are held back by
o: concrete dams built by engineers
walls of ice that form fresh each winter
rock and ice pushed forward by glaciers long ago
the terraced fields along the river
x: The water collects "behind walls of loose rock and ice that a glacier pushed forward long ago". The walls do contain ice, but nothing says they form each winter; they are old.

q: It can be inferred that, before the change in thinking described in the last paragraph, the usual response to these floods was mainly to
o: drain every dangerous lake well in advance
help people after a flood had already struck
move all villages away from the rivers
place sensors on every glacier in the north
x: The new approach is described as the opposite of "waiting for disaster and then rushing in with relief", so the old habit was to respond afterwards. Draining lakes in advance is one of the newer measures, not the old one.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "toll" most nearly means:
o: a fee paid for using a road or bridge
the sound of a bell rung slowly
the damage and loss caused by something
the warning given before an event
x: The floods "cannot always be prevented, but their toll can be greatly reduced": what is reduced is the harm they do. The road fee is the word's commoner meaning but makes no sense here.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards the measures described in the passage?
o: Approving, while admitting that they are not exciting
Doubtful that they can work in such high mountains
Enthusiastic, presenting them as dramatic breakthroughs
Neutral, refusing to judge whether they are wise
x: The writer says the measures are not "glamorous" yet calls them "a sensible shift in thinking", which is approval without excitement. "Dramatic breakthroughs" contradicts "not glamorous", and calling them sensible is a judgement, so the writer is not neutral.

q: The main purpose of the passage is to
o: argue that stubble burning is the only cause of smog in Punjab
describe how weather scientists forecast fog in winter
explain why smog builds up in winter and what this means for reducing it
compare the air of Lahore with that of other cities
x: The passage explains how an inversion traps smoke in winter and ends by saying the only lever is the amount of smoke released. It warns against blaming "a single culprit", so stubble burning is not presented as the only cause.

q: According to the passage, pollution is usually carried away in summer because
o: farmers stop burning stubble during the summer
warm air near the ground rises and lifts the particles
summer rain washes the particles out of the air
factories and kilns close during the hottest months
x: "The ground heats the air just above it, the warm air rises, and the particles are lifted and scattered." Rain may help in real life, but the passage never mentions it.

q: It can be inferred that an inversion is least likely to form
o: on a cold, windless night in December
on a still winter night after a clear evening
on a hot day when the ground is warming the air above it
in the weeks when smog is usually worst
x: An inversion needs cold air near the ground under a warmer "lid", which happens "on cold, still nights". On a hot day the ground warms the air, which rises, the summer pattern the passage describes. The other three choices are just the conditions in which inversions form.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "accumulate" most nearly means:
o: break apart
build up
drift away
cool down
x: The particles are "trapped" and gather "day after day" until they form a thick haze, so they build up. "Drift away" is the opposite: that is what happens in summer.

q: What does the last paragraph do in the passage?
o: It introduces a new cause of smog not mentioned earlier
It draws a practical conclusion from the process explained before it
It questions whether inversions really happen over Punjab
It describes the harm that smog does to people's health
x: After explaining the inversion, the writer says: since "the weather cannot be changed", the only lever is reducing smoke, a conclusion drawn from the mechanism. It adds no new cause and does not mention health.

q: Which best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Canal irrigation should be given up on the Indus plain altogether
Irrigation that cannot drain away makes soil salty, a problem with slow but known remedies
Salt-tolerant crops earn farmers more than wheat and cotton
Frost damages large areas of farmland on the Indus plain
x: The second paragraph explains how waterlogged fields become salty, and the third lists remedies that are "known, though none is quick". The writer never suggests abandoning irrigation, and the frost is only a comparison ("as if dusted with frost").

q: According to the passage, where does the salt in the white crust come from?
o: Sea water that floods the plain in some years
Salt dissolved in canal water, left behind when moisture evaporates
Fertiliser spread on the fields by farmers
Frost that settles on the fields during cold nights
x: "Canal water carries small amounts of dissolved salt", and when moisture "evaporates, leaving its salt behind", the deposit thickens. The frost is only a comparison for how the fields look.

q: Which of the following can be inferred about a field from which water drains away freely?
o: It needs no canal water to grow its crops
It cannot be used to grow wheat or cotton
It will turn white sooner than other fields
It is less likely to build up a salt crust
x: The passage says salt builds up "when fields are flooded season after season and the water cannot drain away", and that drains are a remedy. So a field that drains well is less at risk. Nothing suggests such a field needs no water at all.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "Paradoxically" most nearly means:
o: fortunately
in a way that seems contradictory but is true
as everyone would expect
in exactly the same way
x: The sentence says too much water can make land "as barren as too little", which sounds self-contradictory yet is what the paragraph has shown. "As everyone would expect" is the reverse: the point is that the result is surprising.

q: How is the third paragraph related to the second?
o: The third gives an example that supports the claim in the second
The second explains a cause; the third suggests ways of dealing with it
The third argues against the explanation given in the second
The second describes remedies; the third explains why they fail
x: The second paragraph explains how waterlogging leaves salt in the soil; the third opens "The remedies are known" and lists drains, levelling and salt-tolerant crops. It accepts the explanation rather than arguing against it.

q: Which best states the writer's main point?
o: Tree-planting campaigns waste money and should be stopped
Foreign trees should never be planted anywhere in the country
Schoolchildren should be paid to look after young saplings
Tree-planting campaigns should be judged by how many trees survive, not how many are planted
x: The writer says we should judge campaigns "by what is still standing five years later" and ends: "Survival, not ceremony, should be the measure of success." The writer says plainly, "None of this is an argument against planting."

q: According to the passage, some fast-growing foreign trees cause a problem because they
o: grow too slowly to impress anyone
are eaten by goats more often than native trees
cannot survive their first summer
use a lot of scarce groundwater
x: "Some drink heavily from scarce groundwater." Goats and dry first summers are dangers to any sapling; the passage does not say foreign trees suffer more from them.

q: The writer would most likely praise a campaign that
o: announced the largest number of saplings ever planted in one day
chose foreign species because they grow the fastest
hired villagers to water and guard its trees for several years
planted at whatever time of year suited the officials
x: The writer recommends "paying local caretakers whose job lasts years rather than an afternoon" and "fencing and watering young trees". A record number planted is exactly the kind of figure the writer says "tells us almost nothing".

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "drives" most nearly means:
o: journeys made by car
strong inner urges
machines that turn wheels
organised campaigns
x: "Tree-planting drives" are the events with officials, schoolchildren and announcements, later called "such campaigns". A journey by car is the commoner meaning but does not fit here.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards tree-planting drives?
o: Openly hostile towards the people who organise them
Fully satisfied with the results they achieve today
Uninterested in whether they continue or not
Supportive of their aim but critical of how success is measured
x: The writer calls the enthusiasm "welcome" and says the argument is not against planting, yet objects that "a number planted tells us almost nothing". Calling the enthusiasm welcome rules out hostility.

q: Which best sums up the passage as a whole?
o: The narrator comes to see Nani's thrift as wisdom rather than meanness
Nani refused to buy the narrator a new pencil box
Rubbish heaps at the edges of cities are a growing danger
Families in Multan produce more rubbish today than in the past
x: As a child the narrator thought Nani "simply stingy", but after a lecture on waste "began to see Nani differently" and now copies her habit. The pencil box is one example within that story, not its main idea.

q: What did Nani do with the narrator's cracked pencil box?
o: She replaced it with a new one
She repaired it with cloth and glue
She gave it away to the sweeper
She stored it in her tin box
x: "She fixed it with a strip of cloth and some glue and handed it back." The tin box held buttons, not the pencil box.

q: The sweeper's remark in the second paragraph suggests that the household
o: threw away much less than other households did
had recently moved away from Multan
often forgot to pay the sweeper on time
kept its rubbish hidden inside the house
x: The sweeper asked "whether anyone lived there" because the house "produced so little rubbish", unlike families who "threw them away". The remark was "half joking"; people did live there.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "stingy" most nearly means:
o: careless with belongings
strict with children
generous to neighbours
unwilling to spend money
x: The child thinks Nani is "stingy" because she reuses bags and will not buy a new pencil box, so the word means unwilling to spend. "Generous" is nearly the opposite.

q: Which best describes the narrator's attitude towards Nani at the end of the passage?
o: Admiring, though still a little embarrassed by her habits
Critical of her for refusing to buy new things
Fond of her, but doubtful that her habits made sense
Admiring, with a sense of having misjudged her as a child
x: The narrator "began to see Nani differently", explains her view as "respect", and still opens the tin box before throwing anything away. The embarrassment belongs to the narrator at ten; nothing at the end shows it remains.

q: The passage is mainly concerned with
o: why monsoon rains in Pakistan have become heavier
how tanker water is delivered to city households
how collecting rainwater could ease both flooding and water shortage in cities
the cost of building larger drains in growing towns
x: The passage links floods and shortages, then offers rainwater harvesting as a way to "ease its floods and its shortages with one habit". Tankers appear only as a sign of the shortage.

q: According to the passage, a recharge well works by
o: storing rainwater in a closed tank for drinking
pumping groundwater up to the roof of a house
sending rainwater quickly into the city's drains
letting filtered rainwater sink into the ground
x: A recharge well is "a shaft filled with layers of gravel and sand that filters the water and lets it sink into the ground". The storage tank is a separate option, used "for washing and gardening".

q: The passage suggests that building larger drains on their own would
o: solve both the flooding and the water shortage
do little to stop the water table from falling
raise the water table by holding rain for longer
make rainwater harvesting more effective
x: The shortage happens because rain "races into gutters and out of the city" instead of topping up the aquifer. Bigger drains might carry floods away, but they would still send the water out of the city, so the water table would keep dropping.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "sealed" most nearly means:
o: covered so that water cannot pass through
officially approved
closed with wax or glue
settled finally
x: Soil "sealed under concrete and asphalt" can no longer soak up rain, so the water "races into gutters" instead. "Officially approved" (as in a sealed agreement) is a different use of the word.

q: Which best describes the writer's tone in the third paragraph?
o: Doubtful that the idea could ever work
Realistic but encouraging
Angry at city planners for past mistakes
Strictly neutral, giving no personal opinion
x: The writer admits "No single roof will refill an aquifer" yet calls the idea "too good a bargain to ignore". The words "seems to me" give a personal opinion, so the tone is not neutral.

q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: How Air Conditioners Are Made
The Pleasures of Village Life
Why Deserts Turn Cold at Night
Why Cities Stay Warm After Sunset
x: The passage explains why a city "stays hot long after sunset": stored heat, added heat and too few plants. Air conditioners appear only as one source of heat, not as the subject.

q: According to the passage, plants cool the air partly by
o: storing the sun's heat and letting it out at night
giving off water through their leaves, which absorbs heat as it evaporates
reflecting sunlight back up into the sky
taking in the hot air pushed out by air conditioners
x: Plants "release it through their leaves, and the evaporation of that water absorbs heat". Storing heat and releasing it at night is what brick, concrete and asphalt do, not plants.

q: It can be inferred that, at midnight in summer, a paved square with no trees would most likely be
o: cooler than a nearby park, since concrete loses heat quickly
at the same temperature as the open countryside
warmer than a nearby park
cooled by the heat it stored during the day
x: Concrete and asphalt release stored heat slowly, so they are "still radiating warmth at midnight", and trees cool the air; a bare square would be warmer. The passage says concrete releases its heat slowly, not quickly.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "radiating" most nearly means:
o: taking in
giving off
losing colour
staying still
x: Streets that stored heat all day release it slowly, so at midnight they are giving off warmth. "Taking in" describes what they did during the day.

q: In the third paragraph, the word "Ironically" signals that
o: the writer is joking about people who use air conditioners
the third paragraph contradicts the second paragraph
air conditioners are the main cause of the heat island
a machine meant to cool things down also adds to the heat outside
x: The irony is that a machine "that cools a room pushes hot air outside, making the street a little worse": the result is the opposite of its purpose. Air conditioners are listed with engines and factories, so the passage does not call them the main cause.

q: The writer's main argument is that
o: fertiliser and pesticide should no longer be sold to farmers
a single crop never brings a farmer a good return
small farmers are usually better served by a mixed farm than by a single crop
buffaloes earn more for a farmer than wheat does
x: The writer argues that a mixed farm "spreads these risks" and ends that for a small farmer "steadiness is worth more than the chance of a windfall". The first paragraph grants that a single crop can bring "a handsome return".

q: According to the passage, lentils are useful on a mixed farm because they
o: add nitrogen to the soil
provide fodder for the buffaloes
earn more than any cash crop
protect the wheat from frost
x: Lentils "enrich the soil with nitrogen". Fodder comes from the line of trees, not from the lentils.

q: It can be inferred that the writer would regard a large, wealthy farmer who grows a single crop as
o: certain to lose his land within a decade
unable to buy fertiliser and pesticide
better placed than a small farmer to survive one bad season
immune to pests and falling prices
x: The writer limits the conclusion to "a small farmer, who cannot survive one ruinous season", implying that a richer farmer can absorb such a loss more easily. Nothing suggests that farmer is safe from pests or prices, or certain to lose his land.

q: As used in the last paragraph, the word "windfall" most nearly means:
o: an unexpectedly large gain
fruit knocked from a tree by the wind
a storm that damages the crops
a steady and reliable income
x: A windfall is set against "steadiness" and means the big profit of a crop's "best year". Fallen fruit is the word's literal meaning but does not fit here, and "steady income" is the very thing the windfall is contrasted with.

q: How does the writer treat the single-crop approach in the passage as a whole?
o: Mocks it as an obviously foolish idea
Grants its advantages before arguing against it
Approves of it without any reservation
Admits being unsure what it involves
x: The writer first says "the logic is hard to fault" and lists its benefits, then opens the next paragraph with "Yet" and sets out its risks. Admitting it has strengths rules out mockery, and the later criticism rules out full approval.

q: The writer's chief purpose in the passage is to
o: explain how composting works and why it is better than sending food waste to a landfill
warn that compost heaps can become dangerously hot
describe the life of earthworms and beetles in a garden
argue that every landfill in the country should be closed
x: The passage explains who breaks down the waste and what they need, then contrasts this with a landfill, where waste releases methane. The heat of the heap is one detail of the process, not a warning.

q: According to the passage, a compost heap is turned from time to time in order to
o: cool it down when it gets too hot
push earthworms into the centre
let air reach the organisms inside it
dry it out when it becomes soggy
x: "They need air, which is why a heap is turned from time to time." The passage says the heap cools when the easily digested material runs out, not because it is turned.

q: It can be inferred that a heap made only of fresh peelings would
o: contain no nitrogen at all
never warm up, because bacteria avoid peelings
turn into compost faster than a balanced heap
lack enough carbon for a good balance
x: Peelings are "greens", rich in nitrogen, while carbon comes from "browns" such as dry leaves and cardboard; a heap with no browns would be short of carbon. Peelings are rich in nitrogen, so they do not lack it.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "soggy" most nearly means:
o: too wet
too dry
too hot
too tightly packed
x: The organisms "need moisture, but not so much that the heap becomes soggy", so soggy means having too much water. "Too dry" is the opposite problem.

q: How is the last paragraph related to the third?
o: It repeats the third paragraph's list of conditions in other words
It contradicts the third paragraph's claim that compost needs moisture
It shows what happens to food waste when one condition named in the third paragraph, air, is missing
It introduces earthworms as a solution to the problem of landfills
x: The third paragraph says the organisms "need air"; the last describes a landfill "where air cannot reach" the waste, so it "decays without oxygen and releases methane". Moisture is not mentioned in the last paragraph, so nothing is contradicted.

q: Which of the following best describes what the passage mainly does?
o: It argues that students should be forbidden by their schools from owning phones.
It describes how the games at a fair are designed to keep visitors playing.
It explains why phone alerts disturb concentration so much and suggests a way to limit the harm.
It shows that messages from friends are more rewarding than study.
x: The passage explains why we check every buzz (uncertain reward), what each check costs (switching) and ends with a remedy: "distance". It never calls for a ban, so the second choice goes too far; the fair is only a comparison.

q: According to the first paragraph, why do people check their phones every time they buzz?
o: Most of the messages they receive contain important news.
The vibration is too loud and strong to ignore.
They cannot know in advance which message will be a pleasant one.
Their friends expect them to reply at once.
x: The passage says "we can never tell which buzz will be the rewarding one, we check every time". It says most messages are "dull" and that a phone "does not need to ring loudly", so the second and third choices are contradicted.

q: Which statement would the writer most likely agree with?
o: A glance at a phone does no harm if it lasts only a few seconds.
A student who studies for longer will always learn more.
Strong willpower is the best defence against a buzzing phone.
How often a student is interrupted matters more than how long each interruption lasts.
x: The switching cost "is paid in full every time, however brief the interruption", so the number of interruptions is what counts. The writer says the remedy "is not willpower alone but distance", and the two-hour student achieves less than the one-hour friend.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "thread" most nearly means:
o: a thin strand of cotton or silk
a series of linked online messages
the main danger in a situation
the line of thought being followed
x: A vibration breaks "the thread of a sentence we are reading or a sum we are solving": the line of thought we are following. Nothing is being sewn, and although a chain of messages is also called a thread, here the thread belongs to the reading or the sum.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It applies the idea of the cost of switching to a student's study habits.
It gives an example that contradicts the claim in the second paragraph.
It introduces a new cause of distraction unconnected with switching.
It returns to the comparison with the game at the fair.
x: The third paragraph opens with "This explains why" and shows the student who studies "in dozens of short pieces", each needing a restart: the switching cost of the second paragraph applied to study. It supports the earlier idea rather than contradicting it.

q: What is the writer's main point?
o: Those who invent false stories should be punished by law.
Ordinary people who pass on messages should check them before sharing.
Rumours spread faster in villages than they do online.
Relatives are the main source of false news on phones.
x: The writer argues that "the ordinary forwarders" share the responsibility and proposes a one-minute check before sharing. Punishment by law is never mentioned, and the passage says rumours now spread faster, not more slowly, than courtyard gossip.

q: Which of these does the writer suggest asking before sharing an alarming message?
o: Whether the message has already been forwarded many times
Whether a well-known news source carries the same report
Whether the person who sent it is an older relative
Whether the story agrees with what you already believe
x: The third paragraph says to ask "whether a known newspaper or official source reports the same thing". Trusting a relative and agreeing with one's suspicions are named in the second paragraph as reasons people share without evidence, not as checks.

q: From the second paragraph, it can be inferred that people often share messages:
o: only after checking them carefully against other sources
for emotional or social reasons rather than because they know them to be true
in order to mislead the people who receive them
because they no longer trust any newspaper
x: People forward a message "because it alarms us", because it fits a suspicion or because "it came from a cousin we trust" - feelings and ties, not proof - and "None of these is evidence." The paragraph opens by denying that people forward because they have checked.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "doctored" most nearly means:
o: given medical treatment
dishonestly changed
officially approved
printed in colour
x: A "doctored photograph" sits in a list of false and fake items, so it has been altered to deceive. The commoner meaning, treated by a doctor, makes no sense for a photograph.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards the "ordinary forwarders"?
o: Scornful: they are more to blame than the people who invent the stories.
Fully sympathetic: they are innocent victims of clever liars.
Indifferent: what they share is of little real importance.
Critical but fair: they are partly to blame, and a simple habit could help them.
x: The writer says the forwarders "carry a share of the responsibility too" - a share, so not more than the inventors, who "certainly deserve blame" - and offers a "modest" habit. Saying a false alarm "can cost a great deal" rules out indifference.

q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: A Bank Clerk Loses His Job
What the Machine Could Not Do
How Cash Machines Count Notes
Why Farmers Moved Their Savings
x: The story ends with the point that "The machine could count; it could not reassure": Tariq's value lay in what the machine lacked. He is not dismissed, so the second title is wrong, and the farmers are only one detail.

q: Why did the manager call Tariq in?
o: To tell him that his job was no longer needed
To ask him to help customers who were afraid of the machine
To praise him for coming early and leaving late
To have him trained to repair the machine
x: She called him in "not to dismiss him but to ask for his help", because older customers "were frightened of the machine". Dismissal is directly denied, and his long hours are never mentioned by her.

q: What does the passage suggest about Tariq's fear during his first weeks with the machine?
o: It proved justified, because he was dismissed soon afterwards.
It was shared by the manager, who expected to lose her own post.
It was caused mainly by the rudeness of the customers.
It proved unfounded, because his work changed rather than disappeared.
x: He feared he "would be the next thing removed", but he was kept and became "the person who stood beside the machine". Customers not nodding to him is a detail of the first paragraph; his fear came from the machine taking over his work, and nothing suggests the manager was afraid.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "diligence" most nearly means:
o: polite flattery of a manager
steady and careful hard work
quiet anger at unfair treatment
a written request for help
x: Tariq "came to work early and left late, as if diligence alone could argue his case": diligence is the hard, careful work he hoped would save his job. Nothing in the paragraph shows him flattering anyone or angry.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards Tariq?
o: Mocking of his fear of change
Sympathetic and quietly admiring
Impatient with his slowness
Disappointed by his lack of ambition
x: The writer shows Tariq's worry gently and ends by praising what he gives that a machine cannot: "that he was patient with them". Nothing in the tone makes fun of him, and his slowness is compared with a machine, not criticised.

q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Online and classroom learning have different strengths and work best side by side.
Online learning has made the classroom unnecessary for most students.
The classroom is better than online study in every respect.
School closures did lasting harm to students in small towns.
x: The last paragraph says the two "are not rivals so much as tools for different needs" and advises using both. The second paragraph lists real strengths of online study, so the third choice goes too far; the writer never says online learning replaces classrooms.

q: Which advantage of online study does the passage mention?
o: Confused students are noticed sooner.
Lessons can be watched again at any hour.
A fixed timetable keeps students working.
Classmates help each other through hard weeks.
x: A recorded lecture "can be paused, replayed and watched at midnight". The other three are listed in the third paragraph as strengths of the classroom.

q: What would the writer most likely say about a student who finds it hard to make himself study?
o: He is likely to gain less from online study than from a classroom.
He should study only online so as to build discipline.
He will learn equally well in either setting.
He has no use for recorded lessons at all.
x: Online study helps "a disciplined student", while in the classroom "the fixed timetable does the work of discipline". So a student without self-discipline would get more from the classroom; the writer still recommends recorded lessons for revision, so the last choice is too strong.

q: As used in the fourth paragraph, the word "sustaining" most nearly means:
o: suffering or undergoing
measuring accurately
starting suddenly
keeping up over a long period
x: The classroom is best at "sustaining effort", which the paragraph also calls "the steady push": keeping effort going. The other common sense of sustain, to suffer (as in sustaining an injury), does not fit.

q: What does the word "however" at the start of the third paragraph signal?
o: A conclusion drawn from the facts in the second paragraph
An example that supports the second paragraph
A disagreement with the call for calm in the first paragraph
A turn from the advantages of online study to those of the classroom
x: The second paragraph lists "The strengths of online study"; the third begins "The classroom, however, offers things that are harder to see" and lists classroom strengths. The conclusion comes only in the fourth paragraph.

q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: Free apps should be banned because they collect information.
Advertising on phones is always dishonest and illegal.
Free apps earn money from users' information, a trade users should make knowingly.
Terms and conditions are too long for anyone to read.
x: The passage explains that "The payment is information" and ends by saying users should make "the trade knowingly". The writer says this "does not mean refusing every free service", so a ban is the opposite of the advice.

q: According to the passage, why are advertisers willing to pay for users' profiles?
o: Profiles show them how many people have downloaded an app.
Profiles let them reach the most suitable person at a well-chosen time.
Profiles free them from having to write terms and conditions.
Profiles reduce the cost of building new apps.
x: Advertisers pay "to place their message in front of exactly the right person at exactly the right moment, and such profiles make that possible". Download numbers and the cost of building apps are never linked to profiles.

q: The example of the torch app in the last paragraph suggests that:
o: some apps ask for more access than their purpose requires
torch apps are the most dangerous apps on a phone
users should never give any app a permission
contacts are the only private information on a phone
x: Asking "whether a torch app really needs to see one's contacts" implies that a light has no need of a contact list, so such a request goes beyond the app's job. The writer advises checking permissions, not refusing all of them.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "thin" in "thin in practice" most nearly means:
o: weak and lacking real substance
slim in body or build
spread across a wide area
carefully hidden from view
x: Consent is "real in law but thin in practice" because few people read or remember what they agree to: it exists, but has little real force. The everyday physical sense, slim, does not apply to consent.

q: What does the fourth paragraph do in the passage?
o: It gives a second reason why apps are free to download.
It argues against the claim made in the third paragraph.
It suggests practical steps after the problem has been explained.
It describes how a profile is built from many details.
x: After explaining how information pays for free apps, the last paragraph says what to do: check permissions, switch off location, question a torch app. Building a profile is described in the second paragraph, and nothing in the fourth disputes the third.

q: What is the writer's main purpose?
o: To argue that teenagers should be allowed to play without limits
To warn parents about games designed to make players spend money
To persuade parents not to dismiss all video games as a waste of time
To explain how strategy games are designed and built
x: The writer thinks the verdict "time wasted" is "too quick" and asks parents to watch before "condemning the activity as a whole". The third paragraph admits limits on play, so the second choice is contradicted, and the warning about spending is only a side point.

q: How does the writer describe failure in a game?
o: It is rare and costly for the player.
It is hidden from the other players.
It is usually blamed on a teammate.
It happens often and is quickly followed by another try.
x: Failure is "frequent, public and cheap; the player loses, studies what went wrong and tries again within seconds". "Public" contradicts the third choice and "frequent" the second.

q: Which of the following would the writer most likely agree with?
o: A game that tests only quick reactions offers little of the value he describes.
Playing late into the night is acceptable if the game is a strategy game.
Parents who worry about video games are always mistaken.
Games played alone teach more than games played with others.
x: The value described is planning and handling failure; the writer notes that some games "reward nothing but quick reflexes", so such games lack it. He says "an hour stolen from sleep is an hour stolen, whatever the game" and that he shares part of the parents' worry.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "absorbed" most nearly means:
o: soaked up like a liquid
completely occupied
slightly bored
badly confused
x: A teenager "absorbed in a video game for an hour" is fully taken up by it. The literal sense of soaking up liquid, as a sponge does, cannot apply to a person playing a game.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards video games?
o: Uncritical enthusiasm for every kind of game
Strong disapproval of games and gamers
Amused indifference to the whole question
A qualified defence that admits some real drawbacks
x: The writer defends what good games teach but says "None of this means that every game is valuable" and calls his plea "narrower than it may sound". That rules out uncritical enthusiasm, and the defence itself rules out disapproval.

q: What is the writer's main argument?
o: Families should keep phones away from meals so that real conversation can happen.
Teenagers use their phones far more than their parents do.
Phones are harmful and families should give them up altogether.
Family meals should be eaten in silence to keep them peaceful.
x: The writer proposes "no phones at the table" because "conversation is fragile". He says this is "Not because phones are evil", so giving them up altogether goes too far, and the passage blames adults as well as teenagers.

q: What does the writer suggest doing about a possible urgent call?
o: Letting one adult keep a phone at the table
Leaving the phone to ring in another room where it can be heard
Ending the meal early if a call is expected
Allowing only the parents to answer calls
x: His answer is: "let the phone ring in the next room, where it can be heard." He insists the rule binds "everyone, parents first", so no one keeps a phone at the table.

q: What does the second paragraph suggest about boredom at the dinner table?
o: It is a sign that the meal should be brought to an end.
It is best relieved by watching videos together.
It is felt mainly by the younger members of a family.
It can lead family members to raise matters that truly concern them.
x: A family "never bored together rarely gets past small talk", while important things come up "after the easy topics are exhausted". So the pauses of boredom make room for real concerns; reaching for a screen is what the writer says breaks this.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "surface" most nearly means:
o: rise to the top of water
be made smooth and polished
come out into the open
disappear from memory
x: Worries "tend to surface only after the easy topics are exhausted": they come up and get spoken about. Rising to the top of water is the literal sense, which a worry about an exam cannot do.

q: Which best describes the writer's tone in arguing for the rule?
o: Harsh, blaming teenagers alone for the problem
Doubtful that the rule could ever work
Nostalgic, wishing phones had never been invented
Earnest and hopeful, while expecting some resistance
x: He answers the "Objections" he expects and ends hopefully: families "had more to say to each other than they knew". He makes the rule bind "parents first" and says phones are not "evil", which rules out the second and fourth choices.

q: What is the main subject of the passage?
o: Why news apps and video sites ought to be shut down
Why neighbours so often disagree about the news
How news feeds, by following our clicks, can slowly narrow what we see
How readers can find more stories about football
x: The passage explains how the program shows "more of whatever kept you there" and how "each lesson narrows the next list" into a "bubble". The writer says the program "is not malicious" and puts the answer with readers, not with closing the apps.

q: According to the first paragraph, what does the program study?
o: The user's age, address and family
What the user's neighbours have been reading
Which journalists the user has met
Which items a user opened and how long the user spent on them
x: The program "studies what you have clicked, how long you stayed and what you skipped". The neighbour is mentioned only to say his list is different, not as something the program studies.

q: It can be inferred that the reader described in the second paragraph:
o: deliberately asked the program for more angry stories
would probably be surprised to see how much his feed had changed
regularly compares his feed with his neighbour's
has stopped using the news app altogether
x: He "has not chosen this diet in any deliberate way", and the narrowing is "hard to notice from the inside", so he is unlikely to be aware of the change. The second choice is directly contradicted; nothing supports the last two.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "diet" most nearly means:
o: a plan to eat less in order to lose weight
the regular mix of things a person takes in
a strict daily routine of exercise
a punishment for bad behaviour
x: His feed full of angry stories is "this diet": the steady mix of stories he takes in, as food is taken in. Nothing in the paragraph is about cutting down or losing weight, the commoner meaning.

q: In the second paragraph, what does "this" in "In itself this sounds harmless" refer to?
o: A neighbour seeing a different list from yours
A program arranging the list to match what a user liked before
A reader's love of football
A feed filling up with angry stories over a year
x: "This" points back to the first paragraph's program and its aim "to show you more of whatever kept you there last time". The angry-stories feed is the later "difficulty" that appears "over months", not what "sounds harmless".

q: Which statement best expresses the writer's main point?
o: The chief problem of automation is helping displaced workers move into new work.
Automation should be slowed down by law to protect existing jobs.
Machines will soon leave very little work for people to do.
Young people make better workers than older ones.
x: The writer says "The real danger" is that those who lose old jobs will not gain the new ones, and "What matters is the bridge" between them. He says the total amount of work "has not vanished" and that resisting automation "rarely works".

q: According to the first paragraph, why does the arrival of new machines not end the need for work?
o: Machines break down too often to replace people for long.
People are needed to set them up, fix them, sell them and plan their uses.
Most trades have refused to use the new machines.
Machines can only do work that people find interesting.
x: New machines "create needs that did not exist before: someone must install them, repair them, sell them and design what they will do next". The paragraph says trades "have shrunk" because of machines, so they have not refused them.

q: Which of the following would the writer most likely support?
o: A scheme to retrain laid-off factory workers for jobs in growing fields
A ban on new machines in factories that employ many people
Leaving workers to find new jobs without any outside help
Schools that train each student thoroughly in one fixed trade
x: His "bridge" includes "short, practical courses for adults", which a retraining scheme provides. He says resisting automation "rarely works", that welcoming it without preparation leaves people "stranded", and wants schools to teach students to keep learning "rather than to master one fixed trade".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "stranded" most nearly means:
o: left on a shore by the tide
tied together in strands
left in difficulty without help
moved to a better position
x: Welcoming automation "without preparation leaves many people stranded": out of work with no way across to the new jobs, which is why the writer calls for a "bridge". The literal sense of a boat or person left on a shore does not fit.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude towards automation?
o: Balanced: he sees its benefits but stresses the need to help those it displaces.
Fearful: he believes machines will leave most people without work.
Enthusiastic: he believes automation produces no losers at all.
Resigned: he believes nothing can be done for those who lose jobs.
x: He calls a machine that does a dull job well "a gift" but warns that displaced workers can be left "stranded", and says the outcome "depends on decisions that people... will make" - so he is neither fearful nor resigned.

q: Which statement best sums up the passage as a whole?
o: Life in a village is happier than life in a city.
People should stop posting photographs on the internet.
Cities give people complete privacy from one another.
Online privacy feels uneasy because it mixes features of village and city life in a new way.
x: The last paragraph sums up: online life "combines the village's long memory with the city's strangers, and adds an imbalance". The writer says "Neither arrangement is simply better", so the second choice is not his view.

q: According to the passage, what kept gossip within limits in the village?
o: People knew about one another equally, so the knowledge was balanced.
The shopkeeper refused to discuss his customers.
News travelled slowly from house to house.
Very few people lived close together.
x: Village knowledge "was mutual... and that balance kept gossip within limits". The shopkeeper is said to know who bought medicine, not to keep quiet about it.

q: It can be inferred that a stranger who comes across an old angry post:
o: may judge its writer more harshly than a neighbour who knew him would
knows the full story behind the post
has also seen its writer help at a funeral
will forget the post within a few days
x: The neighbour "also saw you help at a funeral", but the stranger "sees only the post", so he lacks the good side that softens the picture and may judge more harshly. The second and third choices are contradicted, and the internet is said to remember.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "affairs" most nearly means:
o: romantic relationships kept secret
public events and celebrations
official duties in a government office
private business and personal matters
x: "You knew the shopkeeper's affairs as he knew yours" refers back to knowing who bought medicine and whose son failed: everyday private matters. Nothing suggests romance, and the knowledge is about private life, not public events.

q: What does the word "moreover" at the start of the third paragraph signal?
o: That the writer is about to contradict the second paragraph
That the final conclusion of the passage is beginning
That an example of city life is about to be given
That another difference between village and online watching is being added
x: The second paragraph gives one difference: the internet is watched by strangers. "Moreover" adds a second: village knowledge "was mutual", while online "the watching often runs one way". The conclusion comes in the fourth paragraph.

q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Paper gave writers a cheap, light surface, and its spread made knowledge easier to share.
Clay tablets and animal skins remained better than paper because they lasted longer.
Paper was invented mainly to help merchants keep fuller accounts of their trade.
Making paper required rare materials that only skilled craftsmen could obtain.
x: The passage moves from the problem (no material 'both cheap and light') to paper's solution and its effect: it 'made learning far less expensive to share'. Paper was not invented for merchants; their fuller accounts are only one result of its spread.

q: According to the passage, what happens to the fibres as the water drains from the screen?
o: They dissolve completely into the water.
They are baked hard like clay.
They break apart into a soupy pulp.
They bind together to form a sheet.
x: The second paragraph says 'The fibres lock together as the water drains away, forming a sheet'. Breaking into pulp happens earlier, when the fibres are soaked and beaten.

q: It can be inferred from the passage that, before paper, the spread of writing was held back mainly by
o: a lack of people who knew how to read and write
rules that stopped merchants from keeping accounts
the cost or weight of the available writing materials
a shortage of plant fibres in most regions
x: The first paragraph says each material was either heavy or 'slow and costly', and the last says paper made learning 'far less expensive to share', so cost and weight were the barrier. A shortage of fibres is contradicted: the raw material 'was rarely scarce'.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "humble" most nearly means:
o: modest about its own importance
respectful and obedient
plain and ordinary
rare and costly
x: 'Its humble pulp' contrasts the simple, ordinary stuff of paper (soaked rags and bark) with the 'quiet revolution' it caused. The commoner meaning, modest about oneself, describes a person's attitude and does not fit a material.

q: In the second paragraph, the phrase "this double problem" refers to the fact that
o: paper was both hard to make and hard to carry
earlier writing materials were never both cheap and light
clay tablets had to be pressed and then baked
merchants and scholars needed different kinds of books
x: The phrase points back to the end of the first paragraph: 'none was both cheap and light'. Paper is presented as the solution, so it cannot be the problem.

q: What is the writer's main purpose in the passage?
o: To argue that picture writing was more beautiful and expressive than any alphabet
To explain how writing moved from picture signs to sound-based letters, and why that mattered
To describe the daily work of herders who kept records of their animals
To show that people who used alphabets became more intelligent than others
x: The passage traces the change from pictures and word-signs to signs for sounds, then shows its effect on who could read. The writer says the alphabet 'did not make people wiser', which rules out the claim about intelligence.

q: According to the passage, why did the early sign-based systems take years to learn?
o: Readers had to memorise a very large number of different signs.
The meaning of each sign changed from year to year.
Only scribes were allowed to look at written signs.
The signs recorded sounds that people no longer spoke.
x: The first paragraph says they 'demanded years of training, because a reader had to remember hundreds or even thousands of separate signs'. Nothing says the signs changed meaning.

q: Which of the following is best supported by the third paragraph?
o: Traders were the first people to invent an alphabet.
Before alphabets, the ability to read gave certain groups a special position.
Officials tried to ban alphabets in order to protect their jobs.
Once alphabets appeared, everyone in society could read.
x: Reading had been 'the guarded skill of a narrow class of officials and record-keepers', so it set that group apart. The claim that everyone could read goes too far: the alphabet only 'widened' the circle of readers.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "economy" most nearly means:
o: the system of trade and money in a country
the wealth held by a ruling class
the saving achieved by using only a few signs
a cheap class of seats on a journey
x: 'This economy' points back to an alphabet of 'a few dozen letters' that could be learned 'in months rather than years', a saving of effort. The commoner meaning, a country's system of trade and money, does not fit here.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude toward the effects of the alphabet?
o: Hostile, treating it as a threat to serious learning
Indifferent, treating it as a minor technical change
Unreservedly worshipful, calling it the source of all wisdom
Appreciative but measured, praising its benefits without overstating them
x: The writer says it widened 'dramatically' the circle of readers, yet adds that it 'did not make people wiser', a balanced judgement. That same clause rules out the view of the alphabet as the source of all wisdom.

q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: Why Sundials Are Still the Most Reliable Clocks
How Timekeeping Moved from the Sky to Machines
The Working Life of a Town Clockmaker
Candles, Incense and Their Many Uses
x: The passage goes from sun and shadows, to water clocks and candles, to mechanical clocks and their effect on town life. Candles appear only as one of the in-between devices.

q: According to the passage, why were water clocks not fully accurate?
o: Water froze in the vessels on cold nights.
The marks on the side of the vessel faded with use.
A draught made the water drip unevenly.
Water ran out more quickly when the vessel was full.
x: The second paragraph says 'water flowed faster when the vessel was full'. The draught affected candles, not water clocks.

q: What does the passage suggest about early mechanical clocks?
o: Their importance lay less in precision than in giving a whole town a common signal.
They were more accurate than any timekeeping device before them.
They were mostly owned by wealthy families for use at home.
They made sundials and water clocks disappear almost at once.
x: Early clocks were 'not especially accurate', yet once a public clock 'announced the hours', shops and meetings followed its signal; their effect came from being shared. The claim of greater accuracy is contradicted by 'not especially accurate'.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "drifted" most nearly means:
o: floated along on moving water
wandered from place to place
slowly became less accurate
stopped working altogether
x: The colon after 'drifted' introduces the reasons the devices lost accuracy over time: water flowing faster, candles burning unevenly. 'Floated on water' is the literal meaning and only seems to fit because water clocks are mentioned.

q: In the third paragraph, "this" in "Mechanical clocks overcame this" refers to
o: the loud noise made by clocks in towers
the custom of opening shops by the sun
the slow burning of wax and powder
the tendency of earlier devices to lose accuracy
x: The sentence directly follows the statement that 'each drifted', and mechanical clocks fixed this by releasing power 'in equal steps'. The noise of tower clocks is mentioned later and was not something they overcame.

q: Which statement best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Solar calendars are more accurate and should replace lunar ones.
Farmers invented the lunar calendar to plan their harvests.
Calendars were created only to fix the dates of festivals.
Lunar and solar calendars follow different cycles, and each serves different needs.
x: The passage sets out the moon-based and sun-based systems, shows why they do not match, and ends that 'Neither choice is a mistake'. That ending rules out the claim that solar calendars should replace lunar ones.

q: According to the passage, why does a solar calendar add an extra day in some years?
o: To match the start of each new crescent moon
To give farmers an additional day of rest
To make the year equal to twelve lunar months
To correct errors that build up in counting the year
x: The second paragraph says errors creep in 'unless the count is corrected from time to time, which is why solar calendars add an extra day'. The new crescent belongs to the lunar calendar.

q: The passage suggests that a herder with no written tables would find it easiest to keep track of
o: the exact length of a solar year
the extra day added to some years
the passing of lunar months
the date when crops will ripen
x: Lunar months can be checked by anyone 'who looks up at night... without written tables', while the sun 'gives no monthly signal' and its year 'must be counted'. So the solar year is the harder one to follow, not the easier.
