q: As used in the second paragraph, the phrase "creep in" most nearly means:
o: move quietly on hands and knees
are deliberately added by officials
disappear gradually over time
enter slowly without being noticed
x: Errors that 'creep in' unless the count is corrected are mistakes that build up unnoticed. The literal meaning, moving on hands and knees, describes a person or animal, not an error.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude toward the different choices societies have made about their calendars?
o: Critical of societies that allow festivals to move through the seasons
Admiring of solar calendars above all other systems
Puzzled that anyone still uses the moon to count months
Even-handed, treating each choice as sensible for its purpose
x: The writer says 'Neither choice is a mistake' and that each reflects what a community 'most needed its calendar to do'. Accepting the moving festival is listed as one of these reasonable choices, so the writer does not criticise it.

q: Which statement best sums up the comparison the passage makes?
o: Old and modern maps both guide travellers but differ in how they are made and in what they ask of the user.
Old maps were more accurate than phone maps because they were made slowly.
Phone maps should no longer be used because they confuse travellers.
Hand-drawn maps showed every place in the same amount of detail.
x: The passage compares how each map is made and what each demands of its reader, then notes a cost of the newer kind. Old maps are not called more accurate: the writer mentions their 'errors' and the phone map's 'precision'.

q: According to the passage, how did the reader of an old map work out where they were?
o: By following a moving dot on the screen
By asking merchants they met on the way
By matching hills and rivers to the drawing
By zooming in on the nearest street corner
x: The second paragraph says the old map 'demanded that its reader work out their own position by matching hills and rivers to the drawing'. The moving dot belongs to the phone map.

q: It can be inferred that a blank area on an old map most likely showed that
o: the area was covered entirely by sea
the land there belonged to a private owner
the area had been mapped too often to need drawing
the mapmaker had little information about it or thought it unimportant
x: The maker 'had to decide what mattered', and 'empty country was left blank or filled with guesses', so blanks mark places that were little known or thought unimportant. The idea that an area had been mapped too often is the opposite of what the passage says.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "spirits" most nearly means:
o: ghosts of the dead
strong alcoholic drinks
approaches or attitudes
levels of happiness
x: The two maps answer the same question 'in very different spirits', that is, in different ways and with different attitudes, as the rest of the passage shows. Ghosts are a common meaning of the word but make no sense here.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It gives further examples of how phone maps are built.
It points out a drawback of the convenience the second paragraph describes.
It returns to describing how old maps were made.
It disproves the claim that phone maps are precise.
x: The second paragraph shows the phone doing the reader's work; the third begins 'That convenience has a cost'. It does not disprove the phone map's accuracy, because it speaks of the phone map's 'precision'.

q: Which statement best captures the main point of the story?
o: The narrator learned that navigation screens can never be trusted.
Uncle Rashid decided to stop using electronic equipment on his boat.
Fishing trips along the coast are too dangerous for young people.
A night at sea taught the narrator the value of skills that do not depend on machines.
x: The story ends with the narrator noticing that his uncle 'trusted the machine, yet... never let himself depend on it entirely', a lesson he applies to his own life. The uncle used the repaired screen 'for the rest of the trip', so he did not give up on machines.

q: Why did Uncle Rashid switch off the deck light?
o: To save power for the engine
To avoid being seen by other boats
So that their eyes could get used to the dark and see the stars
To make it easier to repair the screen
x: He switched off the light, 'told me to wait until my eyes adjusted, and pointed upward' at the stars. The screen was repaired 'the next morning', not that night.

q: What can be inferred about how the narrator felt when the screen went dark?
o: He was excited to steer the boat himself.
He was angry with his uncle for the broken screen.
He felt uneasy and lost.
He was calm because he already knew the stars.
x: He felt 'the sea grow suddenly larger' and saw that 'every direction looked the same', which suggests unease. He could not have known the stars already, since his uncle had to point out the right one to him.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "modest" most nearly means:
o: shy about one's own achievements
very large and important
simply and decently dressed
not very bright or striking
x: The uncle had to guide the narrator's gaze to 'a modest star low in the north', so it was not an eye-catching one. Shy about one's achievements is the commoner meaning and describes a person, not a star.

q: In the last paragraph, the narrator's attitude toward his uncle is best described as
o: mild disappointment that he went back to the screen
amused pity for his old-fashioned habits
quiet admiration for his balanced approach
lasting resentment at being frightened
x: The narrator notes that his uncle trusted the machine without depending on it 'entirely', and says he has 'tried... to keep a star in view as well', copying him. He reports the return to the screen 'without any fuss', so there is no disappointment.

q: What is the primary purpose of the passage?
o: To argue that modern roads are worse built than ancient ones
To describe the armies that marched along ancient roads
To explain why villages always grew up beside rivers
To trace how roads grew from worn tracks into surfaces built to resist water
x: The passage starts with animal tracks, moves to deliberately built roads whose 'hardest enemy is water', and ends with modern roads that follow 'the same old lesson'. Armies are mentioned only as one reason rulers paid for roads.

q: According to the passage, why did ancient builders give road surfaces a slight curve?
o: So that rainwater would drain off to the sides
So that carts could turn corners more easily
So that armies could march at a faster pace
So that stones of different sizes would fit together
x: The second paragraph says the curve was made 'so that rain would run off into ditches on either side'. Stones of decreasing size were the layers beneath, not the reason for the curve.

q: The passage suggests that, for long periods, well-built roads mainly served
o: farmers carrying their crops to market
the needs of rulers rather than of ordinary travellers
animals travelling in search of water
merchants who paid to build them
x: Only 'rulers who needed to move armies, officials and taxes could afford them', while 'ordinary roads stayed rough far longer'. Animals searching for water belong to the first paragraph's tracks, not to built roads.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "record" most nearly means:
o: a disc on which music is stored
the best result ever achieved
a formal complaint to an official
a lasting trace of past events
x: A road was 'a record of countless small journeys': the worn path is what those journeys left behind. 'The best result ever achieved', as in a sports record, is a common meaning that does not fit.

q: What is the function of the final sentence of the passage?
o: It introduces a new problem that modern builders face.
It links modern roads to the principle that guided ancient builders.
It contradicts the claim that ancient roads were costly.
It sums up how animal tracks turned into roads.
x: 'Beneath them lies the same old lesson: keep the water out' ties today's smooth roads to the ancient builders' fight against water from the second paragraph. It brings up no new problem; it repeats an old one.

q: Which statement best expresses the writer's main argument?
o: Libraries remain valuable because they offer free and equal access to knowledge.
Libraries should replace their books with computers.
The internet has made public libraries unnecessary.
Ancient libraries were more important than modern ones.
x: The writer calls a library 'a promise that knowledge would be available to anyone' and says 'That promise is no less needed today'. The view that the internet has made libraries unnecessary is the one the writer argues against.

q: Which of these does the writer name as people whom public libraries serve?
o: Business owners who need office space
Job seekers who do not have a computer
Publishers who want to sell new books
Officials who manage the city budget
x: The second paragraph lists 'a student without a quiet room at home, a job seeker without a computer, a retired teacher'. None of the other groups is mentioned.

q: If a library began lending laptops, the writer would most likely say that it was
o: changing its methods while keeping its original purpose
admitting that books are no longer useful
making a mistake and should lend only books
wasting money that should be spent on schools
x: The writer praises libraries that 'already lend laptops' and calls such changes 'adaptations, not a confession that the idea has failed'. Treating it as an admission that books are useless is exactly the reading the writer rejects.

q: As used in the last sentence, the word "bargains" most nearly means:
o: goods sold at a low price
arguments about what something costs
secret deals made between rulers
agreements that benefit both sides
x: The library is 'one of the oldest and fairest bargains a community has ever made with its members': an agreement in which the community provides knowledge to all. Goods sold cheaply is the commoner meaning and does not fit.

q: Which best describes the tone of the passage?
o: Neutral and detached, giving both sides equal weight
Nostalgic and resigned to libraries closing
Mocking toward people who still use libraries
Firm and persuasive, defending libraries against a popular view
x: The writer opens by rejecting what is 'fashionable to say' and ends by warning against cities that close libraries, a clear argument for one side. The passage is not neutral: it calls the opposing view a misunderstanding.

q: Which would be the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Counting Boards and Their Pebbles
How Place Value and Zero Made Numbers Easier
Why Merchants Distrusted Written Sums
The Many Symbols of Early Number Systems
x: The passage describes the clumsy older systems, the 'breakthrough' of place value, and zero as its needed partner. Counting boards are only one detail of the first paragraph.

q: According to the passage, what did merchants often use to work out their sums?
o: Long strings of written symbols
Boards with pebbles or beads
Tally marks scratched on paper
A sign that held a place open
x: The first paragraph says 'Merchants often relied on counting boards with pebbles or beads, and wrote down only the answers'. Long strings of symbols were how large numbers were written, which made doing sums with them hard.

q: The passage implies that in the older systems described in the first paragraph, a larger number generally needed
o: more symbols than a smaller number
exactly ten different symbols
a zero to mark its empty places
no written symbols, only beads
x: Numbers were shown 'by repeating symbols and adding them up', and a large sum 'meant long strings of signs', so bigger numbers took more symbols. Ten symbols and a zero belong to place value, not to the older systems.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "clumsy" most nearly means:
o: likely to knock things over
rude and unkind
dishonest and unfair
awkward and slow to use
x: Writing large numbers was 'a clumsy business' because it needed long strings of signs and made arithmetic 'harder still'. 'Likely to knock things over' is the commoner meaning, used of a person.

q: In the third paragraph, the word "But" at the start signals that the writer is about to
o: reject the idea of place value as a mistake
return to the problems of counting boards
point out something place value needs in order to work
compare zero with the use of tally marks
x: After praising place value, the writer says 'But place value has a hidden requirement', a way to show an empty place, which zero supplies. The paragraph does not reject place value; it explains what completes it.

q: Which statement best summarises the passage as a whole?
o: Early medicine rested only on superstition and had no lasting value.
Early medicine mixed mistaken theories with careful observation that later medicine built on.
Modern doctors still bleed patients to restore the body's balance.
Plant remedies are always safer than modern medicines.
x: The passage shows the useful knowledge, then the false theories, then argues that observation 'laid the groundwork for later methods'. The writer says it would be 'unfair to dismiss early medicine as mere superstition'.

q: According to the passage, why did early healers have to guess at the causes of many diseases?
o: They could not see the tiny organisms that cause them.
They were not allowed to examine their patients.
They kept no written records of their treatments.
Their teachers kept remedies secret from them.
x: The second paragraph says 'Because healers could not see the tiny organisms that cause many diseases, they had to rely on guesses'. The passage says remedies were written down and copied, so 'no written records' is wrong.

q: What can be inferred about the practice of bleeding a patient?
o: It came from a theory of illness that the writer regards as mistaken.
Modern researchers found that it contains substances that work.
It was the most effective treatment that early healers had.
Healers gave it up as soon as they saw that it weakened patients.
x: It is given as an example after 'Not all of it was sound', and it 'often weakened the sick'. The substances that 'genuinely work' are found in some remedies, not in bleeding.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "festered" most nearly means:
o: healed quickly and cleanly
were covered with bandages
became infected and grew worse
grew into lasting resentment
x: Wounds that 'festered when left dirty' are set against those that 'healed when kept clean', so they turned bad. Lasting resentment is the word's figurative use, for feelings, not wounds.

q: Which best describes the writer's attitude toward early healers?
o: Scornful of them for lacking scientific tools
Uncritically admiring, ranking their methods above modern ones
Respectful, while admitting that many of their ideas were wrong
Indifferent, since their work has no link to modern medicine
x: The writer admits 'Not all of it was sound' yet praises 'its best practitioners' and says modern doctors continue their 'conversation'. Modern doctors have 'far better tools', so the writer does not rank the old methods higher.

q: The passage is mainly concerned with:
o: why examinations test familiarity with notes rather than understanding
why students should study for longer hours on the night before a test
why recalling material over several days is a better way to study than rereading
how teachers design tests that reduce the amount students forget
x: The writer says rereading gives an "illusion" of learning, recommends "closing the book and trying to recall", and adds that hours "spread over several days tend to last". The passage says the opposite of the idea that examinations reward familiarity: they demand "producing the same ideas from an empty mind".

q: According to the first paragraph, what does an examination demand?
o: Recognising pages that have been read before
Producing ideas without having the material in view
Reviewing all the notes in one long session
Checking notes to see which points were missed
x: The first paragraph says producing ideas "from an empty mind" is "exactly what an examination demands". Recognising a page is described as the far easier task that rereading trains, not what the examination asks for.

q: It can be inferred from the passage that a student who finds recall practice frustrating:
o: should go back to rereading until the material feels familiar
may be studying more effectively than one who finds rereading comfortable
has probably forgotten almost everything she studied
is making mistakes that will lower her examination marks
x: The last paragraph says recalling is "more uncomfortable than rereading" and that "discomfort ... is a sign that the work is doing its job", so frustration can go with effective study. Going back to rereading is the habit the passage calls an "illusion", and mistakes in practice "are not wasted".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "fix" most nearly means:
o: repair after damage
arrange a time for
settle firmly in place
correct a mistake in
x: Pulling a half-forgotten idea back "seems to fix it more firmly" in the mind, so "fix" means to make it stay, to settle it firmly. The commoner meaning, to repair something broken, does not fit, because nothing has been damaged.

q: How does the second paragraph relate to the first?
o: It gives further examples of the problem described in the first
It explains why the habit in the first works better than recall
It offers an alternative to the study habit criticised in the first
It introduces the point about timing that the first paragraph began
x: The first paragraph criticises rereading as an "illusion"; the second begins "a different habit: closing the book and trying to recall". Timing is not raised until the third paragraph ("Timing matters as well").

q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: argue that schools should begin their lessons later in the morning
criticise parents for calling their teenage children lazy
explain why many teenagers sleep late and how the harm can be limited
show that bright screens are the main cause of poor sleep
x: The passage explains the teenage body clock that "shifts later", the shortfall caused by early school, and habits that keep the delay from becoming "a serious lack of sleep". It notes that school "does not shift" but never argues for later lessons, and it says the main cause is "biology", not screens.

q: According to the passage, what happens to the internal clock during the teenage years?
o: It moves to an earlier time
It moves to a later time
It stops working properly
It becomes the same as an adult's
x: The first paragraph says that "during the teenage years this clock shifts later". Nothing suggests it moves earlier or stops working.

q: It can be inferred from the passage that using a brightly lit phone in bed at night is likely to:
o: move the body clock back to an earlier time
have no effect once the body clock has shifted
make it even harder for a teenager to fall asleep early
help a student store what was learned that day
x: The last paragraph says "Some habits make the shift worse" and that bright screens "tell the brain that it is still daytime", so a phone in bed would delay sleep further. The passage gives no reason to think screens reset the clock earlier or have no effect.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "shortfall" most nearly means:
o: an amount by which something is less than needed
a sudden fall from a small height
a late arrival at school
a short period of rest
x: Students "cannot get the long night of sleep that young people need", and "the shortfall builds up over a week": it is the sleep they are missing. It has nothing to do with falling or with resting briefly.

q: In the last sentence, the word "they" in "they can keep a natural delay" refers to:
o: bright screens and long naps after school
teenagers who cannot fall asleep before midnight
the signals that the internal clock sends to the body
keeping a fixed waking time and putting the phone away before bed
x: The sentence names two habits, keeping "a fixed time for waking" and "putting the phone away an hour before bed", and says "they" can keep the delay from becoming a serious lack of sleep. Screens and naps are the habits that "make the shift worse", so they cannot be what helps.

q: The writer's main purpose is to:
o: argue that matches should replace some lessons before examinations
argue that schools should not drop sport to make more time for study
describe how cricket teams recover after a heavy defeat
explain why admissions depend mainly on examination marks
x: The writer says cutting the games period "is a poor bargain" and that a school treating the playground as wasted space wastes "something far more valuable". The last paragraph rules out the idea that "matches should replace lessons".

q: According to the second paragraph, what happens to a student who sits at a desk all day?
o: Concentration weakens as the day goes on
Learning stays steady from morning until evening
Restlessness appears only after a games period
Marks in physics and mathematics improve
x: The paragraph says such a student "does not learn steadily all day" because "Attention sags, restlessness grows". Steady learning all day is exactly what the writer denies.

q: The writer suggests that dropping games before examinations may:
o: make students enjoy games more when they return
be necessary for students hoping for admission
lower the very results it is meant to improve
have no effect on marks either way
x: Sport is cut to raise marks, but the writer calls this "a poor bargain even by the narrow measure of results" and says play restores "the energy to use" study time, so cutting it may harm results. Saying it has no effect contradicts the claim that pupils come back "calmer and sharper".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "sags" most nearly means:
o: grows weaker
hangs down loosely
becomes sharper
grows louder
x: "Attention sags" is listed with restlessness and hours that "produce very little", so attention weakens. The commoner physical meaning, to hang down loosely like a rope, does not fit attention.

q: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as:
o: measured and moderate
angry and accusing
doubtful and uncertain
playful and mocking
x: The writer limits the claim ("None of this means that every student must love games") and calls it "modest", which is measured. The writer is not uncertain: the paragraph still states the point firmly.

q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: The Many Flavours of Pakistani Pickles
Why Fresh Dal Is Healthier Than Pickle
How Bacteria Were First Discovered
How Old Methods Protect Pickles from Spoiling
x: The passage explains how salt, oil, sour ingredients and spices, used by pickle makers "long before anyone could see bacteria", stop food going bad. Flavour is mentioned only in passing, and the passage does not describe how bacteria were discovered.

q: According to the passage, how does mustard oil help a pickle to last?
o: It draws water out of the pieces of fruit
It makes the mixture too acidic for organisms
It keeps air away from the food beneath it
It gives a flavour that organisms avoid
x: Mustard oil "seals the contents from the air, keeping out new arrivals". Drawing out water is the work of salt, and acidity comes from lemon juice or vinegar.

q: It can be inferred that a pickle made with salt and oil but no sour ingredient would most likely:
o: spoil as quickly as a bowl of fresh dal
be fully protected as long as the oil seals it
be less well protected than one made with all of the usual steps
last longer, because acid weakens the fruit
x: The passage says "Each step on its own would protect the food only partly; together they make the jar a very unfriendly place", so leaving one step out gives weaker protection. Spoiling as fast as fresh dal goes too far, since salt and oil still help.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "flourish" most nearly means:
o: wave about dramatically
die out quickly
change colour
grow and multiply well
x: Sour ingredients make the mixture too acidic for organisms "that would otherwise flourish", meaning they would otherwise grow well. "Die out" is the opposite: that is what the acid makes them do.

q: In the third paragraph, the word "then" in "The traditional method, then," signals that the writer is:
o: moving on to a later stage in time
drawing a conclusion from the methods just described
introducing a method that contradicts the earlier ones
giving an example of careless handling
x: After listing salt, oil, sour ingredients and spices, the writer sums up: the method "is not a single trick but a combination". Here "then" means "so" or "therefore", not "after that" in time.

q: The passage is mainly about:
o: why large stores always defeat small family shops
how a young woman persuaded her uncle to lower his prices
how a small shop survived a large rival by offering what the rival could not
why customers felt guilty about shopping on the bypass road
x: Saima "looked for what the store could not offer", namely advice and a plumber, and "The shop is busier now than before". She "did not suggest competing on price", and the shop's survival shows big stores do not always win.

q: What did Saima arrange for Saturday mornings?
o: Lower prices on paint and padlocks
A stall at the store on the bypass
Lessons in keeping the shop's accounts
A local plumber sitting in the shop
x: She "arranged for a local plumber to sit in the shop on Saturday mornings". Lower prices are ruled out, because she "did not suggest competing on price".

q: What does the second paragraph suggest about the customers who "nodded to him a little guiltily"?
o: They were angry that his prices were too high
They felt they were being disloyal to Uncle Rafiq
They planned to return to his shop the next day
They were ashamed of the paint they had bought
x: These were customers "who had bought from Uncle Rafiq for years" and now bought elsewhere; their guilt is about leaving him. Nothing in the passage shows anger or a plan to come back the next day.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "margins" most nearly means:
o: the blank edges around a page
the borders of the main bazaar
the number of regular customers
the profit left after costs are paid
x: Saima sat "over the accounts" after prices were undercut and saw "how thin the margins had become", so the word means the profit on each sale. The commoner meaning, the edges of a page, has nothing to do with the accounts.

q: The narrator's attitude towards Uncle Rafiq is best described as:
o: bitter and critical
fearful and respectful
indifferent and distant
fond and gently amused
x: The narrator praises his memory and personal greetings and smiles at how he "a little grudgingly" lets Saima write the prices down. Nothing is bitter or harsh, so a critical reading is not supported.

q: Which statement best expresses the main argument of the passage?
o: Students should refuse any career that their parents choose for them
Students should base a career choice on real experience of the work, not mainly on prestige
Engineering and medicine are less respected than they once were
Interest in a subject matters more than ability or opportunity
x: The writer calls a choice "made mainly for prestige" risky and says the remedy is "to gather evidence before deciding". The writer says the remedy is "not for young people to defy their parents", and adds "Interest is not everything. Ability and opportunity matter too."

q: What does the writer say about discipline?
o: It is harder to keep up over a whole career than over a degree
It matters more than interest over a long career
It is what families value most in a profession
It is never enough to carry a student through a degree
x: Discipline "is harder to sustain over decades than over semesters". The writer also says a student "may get through a degree on discipline alone", which rules out the claim that it is never enough.

q: The writer mentions "every ordinary Tuesday" most probably to suggest that:
o: most professionals dislike the start of the working week
weddings and family gatherings are usually held at weekends
the daily experience of work counts for more over a lifetime than occasional admiration
prestige is felt more strongly at work than at home
x: The phrase is set against prestige, which "is felt most strongly at a wedding or a family gathering"; Tuesday stands for the plain, repeated days of a forty-year career. The sentence says prestige is felt at gatherings, not at work, so the last idea reverses it.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "shadowing" most nearly means:
o: secretly following someone who is suspected
sitting in the shade beside someone
following someone at work in order to watch and learn
taking over someone's duties for a time
x: "A week spent shadowing an engineer" is one way to "gather evidence before deciding", so it means going along with the engineer to observe the job. There is nothing secret or suspicious about it.

q: The writer's attitude towards families who choose careers for their children is best described as:
o: openly hostile to any influence they have
sympathetic to their wish for security but doubtful about choosing for prestige
fully approving of the choices they make
uninterested in the part they play
x: The writer says families "should not be blamed for wanting security" but that a choice "made mainly for prestige is a risky one". The writer is not hostile: families who encourage experiments keep their influence, which now "rests on facts".

q: The passage mainly argues that city traffic is best eased by:
o: fast, reliable buses, together with easy ways of reaching their stations
building wider roads with more lanes for cars
allowing more rickshaws to carry passengers
making passengers pay their fares on the bus
x: The writer calls moving "more people in less space" with bus lanes "a more lasting solution", and adds that footpaths, crossings and short rides "decide whether a fine new bus line is full". Wider roads "often fill up again within a few years".

q: According to the passage, why do passengers pay before boarding?
o: So that fares can be kept cheaper than rickshaws
So that only regular passengers can use the buses
So that buses spend less time loading at stations
So that drivers can stay in their own lanes
x: Passengers "pay before boarding so that loading takes seconds rather than minutes". Nothing in the passage links paying early to cheaper fares.

q: The last sentence of the passage suggests that:
o: footpaths and crossings cost more than the bus line itself
a well-built bus line can still fail if reaching its stations is difficult
most passengers would rather take a rickshaw than walk
new bus lines in most cities are half empty
x: Small items such as "shaded footpaths" and "safe crossings" "decide whether a fine new bus line is full or half empty", so even a good line can be poorly used. The passage says nothing about these items costing more than the line.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tempt" most nearly means:
o: lead into doing wrong
order by law
warn strongly
attract and persuade
x: The bus must be "quick and reliable enough to tempt drivers out of" their cars, that is, good enough to persuade them. The commoner sense, leading someone into wrongdoing, does not fit, since leaving the car is not wrong.

q: In the last paragraph, the writer regards footpaths, safe crossings and cheap short rides as:
o: a waste of money better spent on buses
unexciting but necessary for a bus line to succeed
a replacement for building new bus lines
amusing details that planners like to boast about
x: They are "dull items in a budget, but they decide whether a fine new bus line is full or half empty": unexciting yet essential. Calling them a waste contradicts "Buses alone are not enough".

q: Which of the following best describes what the passage is about?
o: how a firm improved its work by limiting when messages were answered
why clients prefer firms that reply to messages at night
how an accountant learned to work faster in the tax season
why small firms should refuse urgent requests from clients
x: Nadia's rule that "Messages would be answered at three fixed times a day" led to "fewer errors". Urgent matters "could still be phoned in", so the firm did not refuse them.

q: According to the second paragraph, why did frequent messages cause trouble?
o: Workers had to recover their concentration each time they went back to a task
Clients often sent messages that contained mistakes
Staff spent their evenings replying instead of resting
Messages could be answered only at a few fixed times
x: Returning to a task "after an interruption meant finding one's place and one's train of thought all over again". The fixed times were Nadia's later solution, not the cause of the problem.

q: It can be inferred that, before the new rule, the firm's clients:
o: often complained that replies came too slowly
sometimes received fast replies that were incomplete or wrong
contacted the firm only by telephone
were told plainly what counted as urgent
x: Clients later noticed that replies "now came complete and correct the first time", which implies the earlier quick replies were not always so; the first paragraph also mentions "mistakes were creeping into accounts". Replies used to come "often within minutes", so complaints about slowness are not supported.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "grumbled" most nearly means:
o: praised the change loudly
stopped using the firm
made a low rumbling noise
complained in an unhappy way
x: "Some grumbled at first" is followed by "Within a few months, though", showing an early unhappy reaction that later faded. A rumbling noise is the word's literal sense and does not fit clients.

q: In the second paragraph, "the very responsiveness she had been proud of" refers to:
o: the habit of answering clients' messages at any hour, often within minutes
the care with which accounts had once been checked
the fixed times set aside for answering messages
the staff's ability to finish simple tasks quickly
x: The first paragraph says Nadia "was proud that clients could reach her team at any hour" and that messages were answered "often within minutes". The fixed times came later, as the solution.

q: The chief aim of the passage is to:
o: warn shoppers against buying faulty goods at weekly markets
show that permanent shops are better than weekly markets
describe one vendor's journey around his town
explain how the weekly bazaar works and why it suits traders and buyers
x: The passage says the bazaar "follows a logic of its own" and explains the vendors' low costs and the customers' convenience. Faulty goods are only one drawback, and the passage ends by calling the market "as dependable as any shop".

q: According to the passage, why are a travelling vendor's costs lower than a shopkeeper's?
o: He buys his stock more cheaply than shopkeepers do
He sells only second-hand goods that cost him little
He does not have to carry his stock between sites
He pays for his place only on the days he trades there
x: "Because he pays for a pitch only on the days he uses it, his costs are far lower" than a shopkeeper who pays rent every month. He does carry his stock, "carrying the same stock from site to site".

q: The passage suggests that a buyer who gets faulty goods at a weekly bazaar:
o: may have no way of getting the seller to put things right
can easily return them to the same stall the next week
will find the same goods more cheaply in a permanent shop
has broken the accepted rules of bargaining
x: Goods are "rarely guaranteed, and a stall that sold faulty sandals last week may not return", so the buyer may not be able to complain or get the goods replaced. Easy return the next week is the opposite of this.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "pitch" most nearly means:
o: a ground on which cricket is played
a place where a trader sets up a stall
how high or low a sound is
a talk meant to persuade a buyer
x: The vendor "pays for a pitch only on the days he uses it", and this is compared with a shopkeeper's rent, so it is a trading place. A persuasive sales talk is not something he pays for by the day.

q: The word "Still" at the start of the last sentence signals:
o: a point that holds true despite the drawbacks just mentioned
another drawback added to the ones just listed
a description of something that does not move
a change from the past to the present time
x: After "The system has drawbacks", "Still" introduces a contrast: the market is nonetheless "as dependable as any shop". It does not mean "not moving" here, and it does not add another drawback.

q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
o: a student who learns to cook and comes to value his mother's work
a student who falls ill from food sold at the hostel gate
a mother who refuses to share her recipe with her son
a group of students who start cooking meals together
x: The narrator learns to make dal through several attempts and ends by understanding "how much patient work was hidden in all those ordinary dinners". His mother did share the recipe, dictating it "slowly".

q: What mistake did the neighbour from Swat point out?
o: The onions were burnt black
The flame was too strong
The salt was added too early
The lentils had not been soaked
x: He showed the narrator "that I had used a fierce flame where a gentle one was needed". The narrator was impatient with the onions, but the neighbour's point was about the flame.

q: Why does the narrator think he heard a smile when his mother repeated the advice about salt?
o: She was pleased that his first dal had turned out well
She knew that hostel food usually lacked salt
She believed he would never learn to cook
He had sometimes complained that her food had too much salt
x: The first paragraph says he "occasionally complained that there was too much salt", so her repeated warning was gentle teasing. She dictated the recipe before he had cooked anything, so she could not be pleased with his dal.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "fierce" most nearly means:
o: wild and cruel
very strong
gentle and steady
quickly dying
x: A "fierce flame" is contrasted with "a gentle one", so it means a strong, high flame. The commoner meaning, wild and cruel as of an animal, does not fit a cooking flame.

q: Which words best describe the tone of the last paragraph?
o: reflective and appreciative
bitter and resentful
boastful and proud
anxious and fearful
x: Standing over the pot, the narrator thinks about "how much patient work was hidden" in his mother's cooking, which is reflective and grateful. He admits he "cannot make it taste quite like hers", so he is not boasting.

q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: A young accountant exposes a dishonest senior clerk on his very first day at work.
A new employee is given boring work because his manager does not trust his exam results.
Offices should use machines rather than clerks to check columns of figures.
A dull first task teaches a new employee that careful attention matters more than speed.
x: The last paragraph sums it up: Hamza realised the dull task 'had been a test' and that 'careful attention, not speed' was being measured. Mr. Siddiqui is not dishonest; he suspected the transporter's receipts and wanted fresh eyes to find the problem.

q: What was Hamza first asked to do?
o: Attend an important meeting with the company's transporters
Prepare a report on three months of the company's profits
Compare delivery receipts with the entries in an old account book
Show a junior clerk how to check accounts more quickly
x: Mr. Siddiqui 'handed him a dusty ledger and asked him to check three months of delivery receipts against it'. Important meetings were only what Hamza had imagined, not what he was asked to do.

q: It can be inferred that, before he found the gaps in the receipts, Hamza
o: had been warned about the transporter by Mr. Siddiqui
was checking the figures more slowly than he needed to
intended to complain about his work to the company's owner
did not expect the ledger work to lead to anything important
x: He was 'bored and a little offended' and wanted 'something worthier of his talents', so he saw the task as unimportant. He was not warned: Mr. Siddiqui wanted him to find the problem 'without being told where to look'; and he 'worked quickly', not slowly.

q: As used in the fourth paragraph, the phrase "refuse to agree" most nearly means:
o: decline to accept an offer
fail to match each other
argue with one another
stop being on friendly terms
x: Mr. Siddiqui is speaking of numbers: the receipts 'never quite matched the ledger', so figures that 'refuse to agree' are figures that do not match. Arguing and declining offers are things people do, not the meaning here.

q: Which best describes Hamza's attitude towards his task at noon?
o: impatient and slightly resentful
curious and excited
anxious and fearful
calm and grateful
x: At noon he 'was bored and a little offended' and worked quickly 'eager to finish', which is impatience and mild resentment. He felt worried only later, in the afternoon, when he wondered whether the error was his own.

q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to
o: criticise the training colleges that prepare teachers for village schools
describe the poor condition of school buildings in rural areas
explain why children from farming families often miss school
show how a teacher won a village's trust by linking lessons to everyday life
x: The passage follows Rukhsana's lessons drawn from 'whatever the village offered' and ends with a farmer, once against the school, mending its roof. The leaking roof and absent children are background, and the college plans are put aside without any attack on the college.

q: What did the children do with the school courtyard?
o: They cleaned it before the rainy season began.
They measured it, first in footsteps and then in metres.
They planted vegetables in it for their families.
They used it as a third classroom on sunny days.
x: The second paragraph says the children 'measured the length of the courtyard in footsteps, then in metres'. Nothing is said about cleaning, planting or teaching classes in it.

q: By describing the plastic sheet as "the most honest report on her work", Rukhsana suggests that
o: the district office had refused to read the reports she sent
she had written untrue reports about her school in the past
the farmer's practical help showed her success more truly than an official document could
she should have asked the district office to pay for the roof
x: The farmer had once called the school 'a waste of good working hours'; mending the roof showed that the village now valued it, a proof no written report could match. Nothing says her own reports were untrue or that the office ignored them.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "restless" most nearly means:
o: unable to sleep at night
unable to keep still or pay attention
tired after hard work in the fields
angry with their new teacher
x: The older boys in class were 'restless', one of the reasons the neat lesson plans did not work: they could not settle. The sense 'unable to sleep' (a restless night) does not fit a classroom in the daytime.

q: The writer's attitude towards Rukhsana is best described as
o: quietly admiring
openly mocking
doubtful of her methods
pitying her failure
x: The writer shows her methods working: children check grain weights and read medicine labels, and a doubting farmer repairs the roof. Nothing in the passage mocks her or calls her a failure; attendance rose slowly, but it rose.

q: Which title best suits the passage?
o: The Dangers of Mountain Roads
Why Grandfather Left His Village
A Delay That Made Neighbours
How Bulldozers Clear a Landslide
x: The last paragraph says what stayed with Ayesha was the night 'when a delay had given strangers a reason to become, briefly, neighbours'. The landslide and bulldozers are only the setting, and the passage never says why her grandfather left his birthplace.

q: What did the student going home for the holidays do?
o: He shared tea from a stove he had lit.
He told stories about the valley in the past.
He helped the driver clear rocks from the road.
He started a card game among the passengers.
x: The third paragraph says the student 'organised a game of cards'. The tea came from the family from Mardan and the stories from Ayesha's grandfather.

q: It can be inferred that the grandfather's eagerness during the journey came mainly from
o: his wish to reconnect with a place he had left long ago
his fear that the bus would take a wrong road
his plan to settle in the valley for the rest of his life
his annoyance that Ayesha kept looking at her phone
x: He 'had not seen his birthplace in forty years', made her repeat names of villages 'he half remembered' and told stories of the valley as it once was, all signs of longing for his old home. Nothing suggests he planned to stay there for good or feared getting lost.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "stranded" most nearly means:
o: unable to continue their journey
washed up on a shore
lost in the mountains
tired and hungry
x: The passengers were stuck because rocks blocked the road and they had to wait for the bulldozers, so they could not go on. They knew exactly where they were, so 'lost' is wrong, and the shore meaning does not fit a mountain road.

q: How does the third paragraph relate to the second?
o: It explains what caused the landslide mentioned in the second paragraph.
It shows the delay from the second paragraph turning from a frustration into a sociable event.
It gives the reasons for the journey that the second paragraph leaves out.
It describes the village the travellers finally reached after the delay.
x: The second paragraph ends with Ayesha sulking at the delay; the third shows passengers sharing tea, cards and stories, turning 'the roadside into a small village'. The village they finally reached is mentioned only in the last paragraph, and she 'could hardly remember' it.

q: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: City mechanics are dishonest and overcharge farmers for new engines.
Old engines should always be replaced rather than repaired.
A college education is of no use to a future engineer.
Patient, careful skill solves a problem that a hurried expert had given up on.
x: The company mechanic looked for 'ten minutes' and declared the engine 'finished'; Karim worked 'slowly' and found a fault 'a hurried eye would miss'. The passage does not call the mechanic dishonest, and Imran's last thought compares two days with a year of lectures without saying college is useless.

q: What was actually wrong with the engine?
o: The whole engine was worn out beyond repair.
Its copper tubing had rusted away.
A bracket had snapped off the engine.
A fuel pipe hidden behind a bracket was cracked.
x: Karim 'found a cracked fuel pipe hidden behind a bracket'. 'Finished' was only the company mechanic's mistaken verdict, and the copper tubing was what Karim used to make the replacement.

q: What can be inferred about the company mechanic from the passage as a whole?
o: He did not examine the engine closely enough to find the fault.
He lied on purpose so that he could sell a new engine.
He had no training at all in repairing diesel engines.
He later admitted his mistake to the landowner.
x: He looked inside for only 'ten minutes', and the fault was 'the kind of fault a hurried eye would miss', so his check was too quick. The passage gives no evidence that he lied on purpose, lacked training or apologised later.

q: As used in the last paragraph, the phrase "coughed into life" most nearly means:
o: gave off black smoke and then stopped
was switched on carefully by the farmers
started running with a few rough, uneven sounds
broke down again almost at once
x: The farmers cheered, so the engine started; 'coughed' describes the rough, jerky noise of an engine starting. Nothing says it stopped or broke down again.

q: Imran's silence in the last paragraph most likely shows
o: embarrassment at the farmers' noisy cheering
pride in his own engineering studies
disappointment that the repair took two days
a humbled respect for Karim's practical knowledge
x: He reflects that he 'had learned more about machines in two days of handing over spanners than in a year of lectures', which shows respect for Karim and some humility about his own learning. That thought is the opposite of pride in his studies.

q: What is the writer's main point in the passage?
o: Hiding a small mistake can damage trust in a way that repaying the loss cannot undo.
Students should never lend their belongings to their classmates.
Physics practicals put college students under great stress.
Buying a better replacement is the best way to apologise for a loss.
x: The writer says 'The calculator was easy to replace; what I damaged was harder to name' and that Faraz learned his 'word could not be relied upon'. The better calculator did not settle the matter, so the last option is contradicted.

q: How did the writer behave towards Faraz after losing the calculator?
o: He offered to share his own calculator in the practical.
He explained the loss to their physics teacher.
He kept out of Faraz's way instead of telling him.
He paid Faraz back in cash the same week.
x: The first paragraph says 'Instead of telling him, I avoided him', changing seats and taking 'the long way round the corridor'. He replaced the calculator only 'at the end of the term', and with a new one, not cash.

q: The phrase "while it is still only a mistake" in the last sentence suggests that the writer believes
o: mistakes become impossible to correct after a single day
people forget mistakes quickly once they have been admitted
a mistake that is hidden for long turns into something worse, such as dishonesty
he has stopped making mistakes since his time at college
x: His own lost calculator became a matter of broken trust because he lied ('left it at home') and avoided Faraz; admitting at once keeps it 'only a mistake'. The first day is his own habit, not a claim that later correction is impossible, and he says 'when I make a mistake', so he still makes them.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "settled" most nearly means:
o: made calm and quiet
moved to live somewhere
brought to an end
fixed a date for
x: He thought buying the new calculator 'settled the matter', that is, ended the problem, and then says 'It did not'. The common sense of settling in a new home does not fit a 'matter'.

q: The tone of the last paragraph is best described as
o: bitter and accusing
regretful and reflective
light-hearted and amused
proud and boastful
x: The writer has 'thought about this many times' and admits that he taught a decent person his word could not be trusted, which is regret and reflection. He blames only himself, so 'accusing' is wrong.

q: What is the passage mainly about?
o: The exact steps needed to sew a rilli from beginning to end
How the writer came to see that her grandmother's quilts held the family's history
Why young people today show little interest in traditional crafts
How the writer became a skilled maker of whole quilts
x: The passage ends: 'Each quilt was a family record, and she wanted me to be able to read it.' It gives no full set of steps, and the writer says 'I still cannot make a whole rilli'.

q: What did the grandmother ask the writer to do first?
o: Practise her stitches on a small square of cloth
Sort scraps of old clothing by their colour and weight
Buy new fabric for a quilt from the market
Air the quilts kept in the wooden chest
x: 'For the first week she made me sort scraps of old clothing by colour and weight.' Stitching came only later, 'when I finally made them'.

q: What can be inferred about the grandmother from the third paragraph?
o: She was angry that her granddaughter could not sew properly.
She intended to finish the writer's square of cloth herself.
She expected good work but was patient with her granddaughter's mistakes.
She believed her granddaughter would never learn to sew.
x: She unpicked the poor stitches 'without comment' and let the writer sew them again, then used the finished square in a real quilt: high standards, but patience. Nothing shows anger, and the writer finished the square herself.

q: As used in the last sentence, the word "read" most nearly means:
o: say aloud the words written on
repair the stitches of
understand the meaning of
count the pieces in
x: A quilt has no written words; it is 'a family record', so to read it is to understand what each piece stands for, such as 'a cousin's wedding shirt'. The everyday sense of reading written words aloud does not fit cloth.

q: The writer's attitude towards her grandmother is best described as
o: affectionate and appreciative
critical of her strict methods
cool and indifferent
amused by her old-fashioned ideas
x: The writer remembers her warmly and ends by saying 'I understand now' what she was being taught, which shows appreciation. Her impatience belonged to her twelve-year-old self, not to her view now.

q: Which of the following would be the most suitable title for the passage?
o: Small Attentions at a Roadside Stall
An Accident at the Bus Stand
Why Big Hotels Lose Customers
A Father Who Refused to Rest
x: The story turns on 'these small attentions' that won Sadia new customers and her father's respect. The accident is only the starting point, and the hotel is mentioned once.

q: Why did Sadia prepare cups early for the conductors of the Sargodha bus?
o: Her father had always done it for them.
They paid more than her other customers.
They had only a few minutes at the bus stand.
They wanted their tea with less sugar.
x: The conductors 'had only four minutes, so she began preparing their cups before the bus arrived'. Her father 'had never bothered' with such things, and the less-sugar customer was the old watchman.

q: It can be inferred that Sadia understood her father's formal request as
o: a sign that he recognised and valued her work
a sign that he was still upset about her mistakes
a plan to close the stall on weekdays
a hint that he did not trust the account book
x: He had just looked at the account book and the cups ready for the Sargodha bus, and she understood 'what he could not bring himself to say', that is, praise he found hard to speak. Asking her to help on Saturdays is the opposite of distrust.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "takings" most nearly means:
o: things taken without permission
money received from sales
customers who stopped at the stall
the cost of milk and sugar
x: The takings were 'slightly higher than they had been before the accident' after more drivers stopped, so the word means the money the stall earned. Nothing was stolen, and customers are a cause of takings, not the takings themselves.

q: In the second paragraph, the word "Yet" signals
o: a contrast between Sadia's early mistakes and her careful notice of customers
a reason why Sadia made so many mistakes at first
an example of the habits Sadia learned from her father
a move forward in time to the end of the month
x: Before 'Yet' come her mistakes (burnt milk, wrong change); after it come the things 'she noticed', so it marks a contrast. Her father 'had never bothered' with these things, so they were not his habits.

q: What is the central idea of the story?
o: The old city is too crowded and confusing for children to visit.
A stranger helps a lost boy in a way that also gives back his confidence.
A careless mother loses her son in a busy market.
Booksellers know the lanes of the old city better than anyone else.
x: The ending says the boy 'had been returned not only to his mother but to his own confidence', because the bookseller let him find the way himself. It was Usman who let go of his mother's hand, and the passage makes no general claim about the city or booksellers.

q: Which landmark allowed the bookseller to work out where Usman had been?
o: A shop selling bangles and brass
A mosque with a green dome
A large clock above a man frying samosas
A motorcycle repair workshop
x: Usman remembered 'a man frying samosas beneath a large clock', and 'there was only one such clock in that part of the city'. Bangle and brass shops were everywhere, so they could not identify the place.

q: Why, according to the first paragraph, did walking faster make things worse for Usman?
o: His mother was walking the other way to find him.
The shops around him were starting to close.
The motorcycles stopped him from crossing the lane.
Hurrying carried him further into lanes he did not know.
x: The streets all looked alike, and soon he was in 'a lane he was sure he had never entered', so rushing took him further from where he had lost his mother. The passage says nothing about which way his mother went or about shops closing.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "frantic" most nearly means:
o: wildly worried
very angry
out of breath
calm and patient
x: A mother who has lost her eleven-year-old son in crowded lanes and is searching for him is wildly worried. Nothing suggests she was angry, and 'calm' is the opposite.

q: Which best describes how the adult Usman views the bookseller's decision not to walk him to the clock?
o: grateful, seeing it as a wise and generous choice
resentful at being sent off alone while frightened
puzzled, as he never found out the reason for it
critical of the danger the bookseller put him in
x: He wondered about it 'for years', but 'Only as an adult did he understand the gift', which shows gratitude for a choice that gave him confidence. He did come to understand, so 'never found out' is wrong.

q: The passage is mainly written to
o: show how a difficult night revealed unexpected kindness and skill in a neighbour
warn students about the dangers of studying by a kerosene lantern
complain about power failures on the nights before important exams
explain the difference between two similar chemical reactions
x: The story ends with how wrong Mehwish 'had been about the woman next door', a retired chemistry teacher who spent the night helping her. The power cut is the starting point, not the subject, and the reactions are never named.

q: What do we learn about Mrs. Baig's past?
o: She taught chemistry for thirty years.
She had once been Mehwish's own teacher.
She used to coach the street's cricket team.
She had worked for the electricity company.
x: The third paragraph says 'She had taught chemistry for thirty years.' She could not have been Mehwish's teacher, since Mehwish 'had spoken to her perhaps twice in her life'.

q: It can be inferred that, before that night, most people on the street
o: knew little about Mrs. Baig beyond her complaints
often asked Mrs. Baig for help with schoolwork
knew that Mrs. Baig had taught chemistry
disliked Mrs. Baig because she was strict in class
x: She 'was known on the street mainly for complaining about cricket balls', and the street had 'reduced' her 'to a single complaint', so they knew little else about her. Help with schoolwork or knowledge of her teaching would not fit that picture.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the phrase "the calm of despair" refers to
o: a quiet acceptance that comes from giving up hope
a peaceful mood that comes from being well prepared
the relaxed feeling a person has before sleep
the patience of someone sure that help is coming
x: With no light and three chapters left, she 'decided... that the exam was lost': her calm came from having given up, not from confidence. She did not know help was coming until her brother saw the light.

q: In the last sentence, the writer suggests that the street's view of Mrs. Baig was
o: accurate but unkind
far too generous
based on close knowledge
unfairly narrow
x: To 'reduce' a person 'to a single complaint' is to see only one small part of her, and Mehwish had been 'wrong' about her. The view was not accurate, so the second option fails.

q: Which statement best sums up the lesson of the passage?
o: Steady, patient care can achieve what a short burst of effort cannot.
Officials should never organise tree-planting campaigns.
Neem trees grow well in poor soil even without water.
A retired signalman becomes famous across his town.
x: The campaign planted 'a hundred trees in an afternoon' and most died; the signalman planted a few each season and 'never stopped coming', and the road is now shaded. The passage does not ban campaigns, and few travellers 'know the signalman's name'.

q: What happened to most of the trees planted by the earlier campaign?
o: They died before a year had passed.
They were pushed over by goats.
They were moved to the side of the canal.
They now shade the road to the station.
x: 'Within a year, most of those trees had died.' The goats pushed over the signalman's saplings, and the canal trees are new ones planted by the grown-up boys.

q: It can be inferred from the last paragraph that Baba Ghulam Nabi
o: was hurt that travellers did not thank him
had told the boys to plant trees along the canal
hoped the road would one day be named after him
did not want praise or fame for his work
x: Few travellers know his name, 'which, his neighbours say, is exactly how he would have wanted it', so he did not seek credit. Wanting the road named after him is the opposite, and the passage does not say he sent the boys to the canal.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "sceptical" most nearly means:
o: unfriendly
excited
doubtful
rude
x: People were 'polite but sceptical' and asked why one old man 'would succeed where an entire campaign had failed', so they doubted him. 'Polite' rules out unfriendly or rude.

q: In the third paragraph, "The answer" is the answer to which question?
o: How one old man could succeed where a whole campaign had failed
Why the campaign's officials never came back to the road
How the boys could carry water without wasting it
Why travellers do not know the signalman's name
x: The second paragraph ends with the question 'Why... would one old man succeed where an entire campaign had failed?', and the third begins 'The answer... was that he never stopped coming'. The mud rings come later in the paragraph and are not a question.

q: The writer's main purpose in the passage is to:
o: call for written exams to be abolished in Pakistani schools
explain how examination papers are set and marked each year
warn students that cheating in exam halls is becoming common
argue that final grades should combine exam results with other assessed work
x: The writer says "I do not want to abolish it" and proposes that "a modest share of the final grade could come from projects", placing exams "beside other evidence". Abolishing exams is the very thing the writer rejects.

q: Which reason does the writer give for the popularity of written exams?
o: They cost little to run and are the same for every candidate
They measure every kind of ability with equal fairness
They allow teachers to reward their own favourite pupils
They were designed by universities to sort applicants
x: The first paragraph says a written exam is "cheap to run, the same for everyone". The writer argues the opposite of exams measuring every ability: a timed paper "rewards a particular talent".

q: Which of these would the writer most likely support?
o: Replacing all final exams with projects marked only by pupils' own teachers
Letting each teacher decide final grades without any outside check
A science grade that partly reflects a term-long experiment checked by outside moderators
Making every exam paper longer so that it can test more skills
x: The writer wants "a modest share" of the grade from projects, "checked by outside moderators", and praises the student who designs "a careful experiment over six weeks". Replacing exams entirely goes against "The remedy is not to throw exams away".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "wither" most nearly means:
o: dry out for lack of water
weaken and fade away
grow more confident
turn bitter
x: Abilities "quietly wither" because students "stop spending time on what is never rewarded", so they weaken and fade. Drying out for lack of water is the word's literal meaning for plants, not its meaning here.

q: The writer's attitude towards written exams is best described as:
o: entirely hostile to them as a way of judging students
accepting of their value but critical of relying on them alone
admiring of them as a complete measure of ability
uninterested in whether they are used or not
x: The writer lists their strengths and says "I do not want to abolish it", but objects to "pretending that it tells us everything". This rules out entire hostility as well as full admiration.

q: Which title best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Why Homework Should Be Banned at Once
The Problem Is the Amount, Not the Idea
How Parents Can Help With Worksheets
The Long History of School Discipline
x: The writer says "The trouble is not homework itself but its sheer bulk" and suggests short, planned tasks with comments. A ban is not proposed, since short tasks are praised as fixing skills "in memory".

q: According to the passage, what do some tired children do when they have too much homework?
o: Refuse to eat until the work is finished
Ask their teachers to compare notes
Stay home from school the next day
Hand the difficult parts to an older brother or sister
x: The second paragraph says tired children "let an older sibling do the hard parts". Teachers comparing notes is the writer's remedy, not something children do.

q: The writer implies that, at present, teachers of the same class:
o: set far too little homework
write detailed comments on all homework
do not plan their homework together
have stopped giving tests
x: Homework is "set by six teachers who never compare notes", and the writer suggests they "might agree on a weekly timetable", so they do not plan together now. Detailed comments are what the writer asks for, implying they are missing.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the phrase "tempers fray" most nearly means that people:
o: unravel into loose threads
become strained and irritable
grow calm and patient
fall quietly asleep
x: Parents "hover" over a long, tiring evening of work, so their tempers become strained. Unravelling into threads is what fraying cloth does, not tempers.

q: The writer's attitude towards the claim that heavy homework builds discipline is:
o: sceptical, suggesting it can even produce the reverse
fully persuaded, wanting more such homework
indifferent, treating it as unimportant
angrily dismissive of all homework of any kind
x: The writer says "I am not convinced" and ends by calling unread work "the very opposite of discipline". The writer is not against all homework, since a short task "can fix it in memory".

q: The passage is mainly about:
o: why old shopfronts in crowded bazaars should be demolished to widen lanes
how a town eased crowding in its old market by keeping cars out and offering other ways in
how small electric rickshaws are built and run in Punjab towns
the history of trade in Noorpur's bazaar over a hundred years
x: The passage describes the problem, the committee's car ban with a car park and rickshaws, and the result. Demolishing shopfronts is the option the committee turned down.

q: Under the new arrangement, deliveries to the bazaar:
o: could be made only early in the morning
were banned at all times of day
had to be carried in by electric rickshaws
could be made between ten and eight
x: The second paragraph says "Deliveries were allowed only in the early morning." The rickshaws carried shoppers and their bags, and ten to eight were the hours when cars were barred.

q: What can be inferred about the traders who protested in the first weeks?
o: Their fear of losing customers was not borne out by what followed
They persuaded the committee to let cars back in
They were the ones who first asked for the car ban
They wanted the committee to build more car parks in the bazaar
x: The traders "feared ruin", yet "within a few months the number of shoppers had risen", so their fear proved unfounded. Nothing suggests the ban was lifted; the writer presents it as a lesson other towns should copy.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "linger" most nearly means:
o: wait impatiently in a queue
leave as soon as possible
stay on without hurrying away
bargain loudly over prices
x: Families began "to stroll and linger", spending unhurried time in the bazaar. Leaving quickly is the opposite of this meaning.

q: What does the third paragraph mainly do?
o: It reports how the change worked out and draws a general lesson from it
It describes the traffic problem the bazaar faced before any change
It lists the separate parts of the committee's plan
It argues that the main lane should have been widened after all
x: The paragraph tells how shoppers returned "within a few months" and then says "This is the lesson other towns should take". The problem is described in the first paragraph and the plan in the second.

q: Which statement best expresses the writer's main point?
o: The valley should be closed to visitors to protect its natural beauty
Tourism has brought nothing but benefits to the people of the valley
Tourism in the valley should be controlled so that it helps local people without ruining the place
A wider highway is needed so that more visitors can reach the valley
x: The writer says "The answer is not to close the valley but to manage it" and wants local families to "share in the earnings". Closing the valley is directly rejected.

q: According to the writer, much of the money that tourism brings:
o: goes to businesses that are based outside the valley
is spent on collecting waste from the streams
is shared fairly among the village families
is used to keep the highway in good repair
x: The money "flows to hotel owners and tour companies from the cities". Spending an entry fee on waste collection is the writer's proposal, not what happens now.

q: The writer would most likely agree that the villagers of Chinar Dara:
o: should not be allowed to earn money from visitors
are mainly to blame for the litter in the streams
want the valley closed to all outsiders
ought to gain more from tourism than they do at present
x: The writer complains that villagers are "left with the litter, the noise and rising prices" and proposes keeping licences for local families. The writer defends their right not to "stay poor", so barring them from earning is contradicted.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "drift" most nearly means:
o: float slowly along
sink to the bottom
break into pieces
pile up on the bank
x: Plastic bottles "drift in the streams", carried slowly by the water. Sinking is the opposite of what floating bottles do.

q: How does the writer treat the argument that tourism is the valley's only hope?
o: With scorn, as an argument not worth discussing
With complete agreement, as the strongest point in the debate
With respect, while showing that it leaves out an important fact
With confusion, unable to decide whether it is true
x: The writer says "That argument deserves respect. But much of the money does not stay in the valley." This rules out scorn as well as complete agreement.

q: The writer's main point is that:
o: printed books are better than screens for every purpose
phones should be kept away from students while they study
paper and screens each suit different kinds of reading
screens will soon replace printed books entirely
x: The last paragraph says "Neither medium, then, is simply better" and advises choosing "the tool that fits the task". Paper being better for every purpose is denied by this sentence.

q: Which advantage of screens does the passage mention?
o: They help readers remember where an argument appeared
They never interrupt the reader with messages
They cost much less than printed books
Text can be made larger for readers with tired eyes
x: The first paragraph says a text "can be enlarged for tired eyes". Remembering where an argument sat on the page is an advantage of paper, given in the second paragraph.

q: Which advice would the writer most likely give a student studying a long, difficult textbook for an exam?
o: Study it in printed form if possible
Read it on a phone so that it can be searched
Skip it and read short articles instead
Read it on a screen with messages switched on
x: The writer says "paper suits long, demanding reading that must be understood and remembered" and keeps "the chemistry textbook open on the desk". Searching on a phone is linked only to "quick searching", not to long study.

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "medium" most nearly means:
o: a size between small and large
an average level of skill
a kind of careful reader
a means by which writing reaches the reader
x: "Neither medium" refers to paper and screen, the two means of presenting text. The common meaning of a middle size does not fit the comparison.

q: The word "however" in the first sentence of the second paragraph signals:
o: a result that follows from the advantages of screens
a further example of what screens can do
a repetition of the passage's opening question
a turn from the advantages of screens to those of paper
x: The first paragraph lists what screens offer; the second begins "Paper, however, has strengths", turning to the other side. It does not continue the list of screen advantages.

q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Competition harms every pupil and should be removed from schools
Cooperation lets weak pupils copy and should be avoided
Competition and cooperation both have strengths and weaknesses, and good schools combine them
Schools should post rankings every month to raise effort
x: The second paragraph says "each has a point" and gives drawbacks of each, and the third says "The wisest schools seem to borrow from both." The claim that competition harms every pupil ignores its power to "spur effort".

q: In the second school described in the first paragraph, pupils are:
o: given prizes if they come in the top three
ranked every month on the noticeboard
praised for helping classmates who find the work harder
tested only against their own last result
x: The second school praises children "for helping a slower classmate". Prizes and monthly rankings belong to the first school, and testing against one's own last result is from the third paragraph.

q: Which feature of the "wisest schools" would most directly deal with the problem of a "careless group"?
o: Letting pupils measure themselves against a fixed standard
Posting the names of the best pupils on the noticeboard
Giving each member a part of the task that can be seen and checked
Allowing the strongest member to do most of the work
x: In a careless group "the strongest member may do all the work"; tasks where "every member has a part that can be seen and checked" stop others drifting on "borrowed credit". A fixed standard deals with pupils being measured against each other, not with group work.

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "spur" most nearly means:
o: slow down
measure
stimulate
wound
x: Competition can "spur effort": a pupil seeing a rival's name "may study harder", so it stimulates effort. "Wound" reflects the sharp spur on a rider's boot, not the meaning here.

q: How is the second paragraph mainly organised?
o: It sets out a benefit and a drawback of each approach in turn
It describes two schools one after the other
It tells the story of a single pupil's year
It lists the steps a school should follow to change
x: It gives competition's benefit ("spur effort") and drawback (some "may simply give up"), then cooperation's benefit ("patience and teamwork") and drawback ("a careless group"). The two schools are described in the first paragraph.

q: The writer's main purpose is to:
o: explain why fewer people borrow books in small towns
describe how public libraries are designed and built
show that phones can now do everything a library does
argue that the town's library should be kept and improved rather than closed
x: The writer calls the case for closing "tidy, and it is wrong" and urges "reviving it" with evening hours and computers. The writer denies that phones do everything: "it does not offer a desk, a silence or a guide".

q: Which reason did the councillors give for closing the library?
o: The librarian was about to retire
Local schools refused to send pupils there
The library was too noisy for study
The roof of the building would be expensive to repair
x: The first paragraph says "the building's roof needed costly repairs". The library is described as "quiet", and the writer suggests schools be invited, not that they refused.

q: The writer implies that the low borrowing figures:
o: prove that the town no longer needs a library
were caused by the damaged roof
are lower than the councillors believe
may partly result from the way the library has been run
x: Falling borrowing "may simply show that the library has been neglected: its hours cut, its stock never renewed". The writer says outright that it is not "a sign that the need has gone".

q: As used in the second paragraph, the word "tidy" most nearly means:
o: free of dust and clutter
neat and convincing on the surface
long and carefully detailed
rude and careless
x: "The argument is tidy, and it is wrong": it looks neat and persuasive but fails. "Free of dust and clutter" is the word's ordinary meaning for a room, not an argument.

q: The final sentence of the passage suggests that the writer feels:
o: anger at the librarian for neglecting the building
concern for people who rely on the library but have little voice
amusement at the councillors' simple reasoning
indifference to whether the library stays open
x: The writer warns that "those who suffer most from its absence are the ones least able to complain", showing concern for such people. The neglect is not blamed on the librarian, who is praised for knowing "her readers".

q: Which title best fits the passage?
o: How to Repair an Old Radio
Why New Gadgets Are Always Better
Mending Is Sensible, Not Shameful
A Short History of the Bazaar
x: The writer argues that "Fixing a thing is not a sign of poverty. It is a small act of good sense". The radio story is only an opening example, not a set of repair instructions.

q: Which hidden cost of cheap new gadgets does the writer mention?
o: Higher electricity bills for the people who use them
The wages that must be paid to repairers
Heavy taxes on goods brought from abroad
Harm to the soil from electronics that have been thrown away
x: The second paragraph lists "heaps of discarded electronics that leak poisons into the soil". Repairers' wages are not presented as a cost of new gadgets.

q: Which of these would the writer most likely approve of?
o: A shop that offers half price on a new blender when the old one breaks
A phone maker that sells replacement batteries and screens
A school that drops all its practical lessons
A buyer who replaces a phone every year
x: The writer asks makers "to sell spare parts" and wants products "that can be opened and mended". A discount on a new blender encourages the habit the writer criticises: "We throw it away and buy another."

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "dwindling" most nearly means:
o: quickly growing
becoming famous
gradually shrinking
moving abroad
