x: The repairers' trade "is dwindling", and the writer asks us to "support them", so it is getting smaller. Growing is the opposite.

q: The tone of the final paragraph is best described as:
o: bitterly accusing
coldly technical
playfully mocking
warmly persuasive
x: The writer praises repairers as "skilled people", suggests gentle steps, and ends with repair as "respect for the effort that went into making it". Nobody is attacked, so "bitterly accusing" does not fit.

q: What is the writer's main argument?
o: Young people should avoid going to university altogether
Skilled trades deserve far more respect and support than they now receive
Every tradesperson earns more than every graduate
Medicine and engineering already have too many students
x: The writer calls the low view of trades "costly" and wants a society that "respects the people who build and mend its world". The passage says only that a plumber "may earn more than a graduate stuck in a poorly paid clerical post", not that every tradesperson does.

q: According to the passage, what do technical colleges need?
o: More students who did badly at school
Teachers who have worked in the trades they teach
Fewer practical lessons and more lectures
Higher fees to pay for their buildings
x: The third paragraph says colleges need "teachers who have actually worked in their trades". None of the other needs is mentioned.

q: The writer's objection to phrases like "only a mechanic" suggests a belief that:
o: everyday speech helps keep skilled trades looking second-rate
mechanics and tailors use the word too often themselves
tradespeople are paid only for their certificates
parents seldom talk with their children about careers
x: The writer links "stop using the word 'only'" to building a society that "respects" tradespeople, so such speech belittles their work. Pay for certificates is a separate point about employers, and it is not limited to tradespeople.

q: As used in the first paragraph, the word "steered" most nearly means:
o: made to drive a vehicle
guided in a particular direction
forced by law
kept away
x: A child who does well "is steered towards medicine or engineering", that is, guided that way by the family. Driving a vehicle is the word's ordinary meaning, not its meaning here.

q: How does the writer regard the idea that a trade is "the fallback"?
o: As a sensible judgement by caring parents
As an amusing old saying
As an unfair view of valuable work
As a question the writer cannot settle
x: The writer says "This attitude is costly" and compares the electrician to office workers who "earn far more respect". The writer clearly rejects the view, so it is not seen as sensible or unsettled.

q: What is the writer mainly trying to persuade readers to do?
o: record the memories of older relatives before they are lost
stop trusting official records, which are useless to historians
find out how weddings were arranged sixty years ago
learn how to use a phone to record sound
x: The writer says "we must listen to the people who lived them while we still can" and suggests recording interviews. Official sources are called "valuable", so "useless" is too strong.

q: According to the passage, official papers mostly tell us about:
o: people who had power or who wrote for a living
farmers, potters and ordinary households
the songs sung at village weddings
children growing up in large families
x: The second paragraph says they tell us "mostly about people who held power or who wrote for a living". Farmers and potters are the ones who "left few documents behind".

q: When the writer says the task is not difficult, "and that is precisely why it is so often neglected", the suggestion is that:
o: because it is easy, the memories it gathers are of little value
because it is easy, people feel it can always be done later
people lack the equipment needed to record interviews
older relatives usually refuse to answer questions
x: The task is easy, yet memories "vanish" when people die, so easy jobs get put off until too late. Lack of equipment is contradicted: "A phone can record an hour of talk". The writer insists the memories are valuable: an imperfect memory "is still worth more than one that is lost".

q: As used in the third paragraph, the word "coloured" most nearly means:
o: painted in bright shades
made more accurate
influenced and slightly distorted
made shorter
x: Recollections "coloured by age and affection" are called "unreliable", so they are influenced and bent by feeling. Painting in bright shades is the literal meaning, which does not apply to memories.

q: How does the writer respond to the objection that such recollections are unreliable?
o: The writer rejects it as completely false
The writer accepts it and drops the proposal
The writer admits it is partly true but argues it does not cancel their value
The writer ignores it and changes the subject
x: The writer answers "They are, but so are many official records" and says an imperfect memory "is still worth more than one that is lost". Saying "They are" rules out rejecting it as false.
